topics.name: Introduction to Microservices

beginner.content:
What is a Microservice?

A microservice is a small, independently deployable service that implements a single business capability and communicates with other services over a network, typically via HTTP/REST or messaging. A microservices architecture is a style of building an application as a suite of such services, rather than one large deployable unit.

Where It Came From

• Early enterprise apps were built as monoliths - one codebase, one deployable artifact (a WAR/JAR), one database.
• SOA (Service-Oriented Architecture) in the 2000s introduced the idea of splitting a system into services, but usually with a heavyweight shared bus (ESB) and coarse-grained services.
• Microservices (the term popularized around 2011-2014, notably by companies like Netflix and Amazon) pushed this further - fine-grained services, each owning its own data, deployed and scaled independently, with lightweight communication (REST/messaging instead of a heavyweight ESB).

Key Characteristics

• Small and focused - each service does one thing (e.g. "Order Service", "Payment Service", "Inventory Service").
• Independently deployable - you can deploy a change to the Payment Service without redeploying the entire application.
• Owns its own data - each service typically has its own database; other services never reach directly into it.
• Organized around business capability - services are split by what the business does (orders, payments, shipping), not by technical layer (UI, logic, data).
• Communicates over the network - via REST, gRPC, or asynchronous messaging, since services run as separate processes (often on separate machines/containers).

expert.content:
The Honest Tradeoffs

Microservices are frequently sold as an unambiguous upgrade over monoliths - they aren't. They trade one set of problems for another.

What You Gain

• Independent deployability - ship a fix to one service without a full-system release.
• Independent scalability - scale only the service under load (e.g. Checkout during a sale), not the whole app.
• Team autonomy - different teams own different services, choose their own release cadence, even their own tech stack.
• Fault isolation - (if done right) one service crashing doesn't necessarily take down the whole system.

What It Costs You

• Operational complexity - you now have N deployables, N sets of logs, N things that can be down, instead of one.
• Network latency and failure modes - an in-process method call becomes a network call, which can be slow or simply fail (the network is not reliable).
• Distributed debugging - a single user request may touch 6 services; tracing what went wrong requires distributed tracing tooling, not just a stack trace.
• Data consistency challenges - no more simple cross-table SQL joins/transactions across services owning different data (see Distributed Data Management).
• Testing complexity - integration/end-to-end tests now need multiple services running together.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a microservice?A small, independently deployable service implementing one business capability, communicating with others over the network
How do microservices differ from SOA?SOA typically used a heavyweight shared ESB and coarser services; microservices favor fine-grained services with lightweight REST/messaging and no central bus
Name two real costs of microservices, not just benefitsOperational complexity (many deployables to run/monitor) and distributed debugging (a single request spans multiple services, requiring tracing tools)
Why do microservices typically own their own database?To keep each service independently deployable and loosely coupled - shared databases create hidden coupling between services

topics.name: Monolithic vs Microservices Architecture

beginner.content:
Monolith vs Microservices

A monolith is a single deployable unit containing all of an application's functionality - one codebase, one build, one deployment, usually one database. A microservices architecture splits that same functionality across many independently deployable services.

Comparison

AspectMonolithMicroservices
Deployment unitOne (whole app deployed together)Many (each service deployed independently)
DatabaseUsually one shared databaseTypically one database per service
ScalingScale the entire app, even if only one part is under loadScale just the service under load
Team structureOne team (or many teams sharing one codebase)Small teams, each owning one or a few services
Technology choiceOne stack for the whole appEach service can use a different stack (polyglot)
Operational overheadLow - one thing to deploy/monitorHigh - many things to deploy/monitor/secure
Cross-feature transactionsSimple - one local DB transactionHard - needs patterns like Saga (see Microservices Design Patterns course)

expert.content:
"Monolith First" - The Migration Strategy

A well-known piece of advice (popularized by Martin Fowler) is: start with a monolith, and only split into microservices once you actually feel the pain that microservices solve.

Why Start With a Monolith

• Early on, the business domain isn't well understood yet - it's hard to draw good service boundaries before you know where they should be.
• A monolith is simpler to build, test, deploy, and debug - which matters most when a small team is moving fast and the product itself is still changing.
• Splitting too early, along the wrong boundaries, creates a "distributed monolith" - all the operational cost of microservices, none of the independence benefit, because services still have to change together.

When Microservices Start Paying Off

• The team has grown large enough that multiple teams stepping on each other's toes in one codebase is a real bottleneck.
• Specific parts of the system need very different scaling profiles (e.g. a recommendation engine needs way more compute than the user-profile service).
• Domain boundaries have become clear enough (often via Domain-Driven Design's "bounded contexts") to split along seams that will stay stable.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
When is a monolith the right choice?Small teams, early-stage products, or when domain boundaries aren't well understood yet - simplicity beats independence at that stage
What is a "distributed monolith"?A microservices split done along the wrong boundaries - services still have to change together, so you get microservices' operational cost without their independence benefit
What does "monolith first" advise?Start with a monolith and split into microservices only once you feel real pain (team scale, differing scaling needs) that justifies the added operational complexity

topics.name: Core Characteristics of Microservices

beginner.content:
What Makes a Service "Micro"

Not every small service is automatically well-designed - certain characteristics distinguish a well-built microservice from just "a small program that happens to run separately":

• Single Responsibility - a service should do one thing and do it well (one bounded business capability), not several unrelated things bundled together.
• Decentralized Data Management - each service owns its own database/schema; no other service reaches directly into it. Data is only accessed through the owning service's API.
• Independent Deployability - a service can be deployed on its own schedule, without coordinating a release with every other service.
• Technology Heterogeneity (Polyglot) - one service can be written in Java/Spring Boot, another in Node.js, another in Go - each team picks what fits their service best.
• Failure Isolation - one service failing shouldn't (ideally) cascade and take down every other service (this is why patterns like Circuit Breaker exist - see the Microservices Design Patterns course).
• Smart Endpoints, Dumb Pipes - business logic lives inside the services themselves; the communication mechanism between them (HTTP, a message broker) stays simple, not a heavyweight orchestration engine.

expert.content:
Sizing a Service - "Micro" Doesn't Mean "Tiny"

A common beginner misconception is that "microservice" means "as small as possible" (e.g. one service per database table). In practice, the right size is driven by bounded context (a Domain-Driven Design concept) - a service should be exactly as big as one coherent business capability, no bigger and no smaller.

Splitting too finely creates "nanoservices" - services so small that most requests still need to call 5+ other services, multiplying the network-latency and failure-mode costs described in the Introduction topic, without a matching benefit.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does "decentralized data management" mean?Each service owns its own database; other services can only reach that data through the owning service's API, never directly
What does "smart endpoints, dumb pipes" mean?Business logic lives in the services themselves; the communication layer (HTTP/message broker) stays simple rather than embedding orchestration logic
Why is "as small as possible" the wrong sizing goal?Splitting too finely creates "nanoservices" where most requests fan out across many services, multiplying network/failure costs without a matching benefit - size should follow bounded context, not an arbitrary smallness target

topics.name: Inter-Service Communication

beginner.content:
How Services Talk to Each Other

Since each microservice runs as a separate process, they must communicate over the network. There are two broad styles:

• Synchronous - the caller sends a request and waits/blocks for a response (REST over HTTP, or gRPC for a faster, typed, binary protocol).
• Asynchronous - the caller sends a message/event and moves on without waiting for an immediate response (via a message broker - see the Integration & Messaging Patterns course for the full catalog).

expert.content:
Choosing Between Styles

AspectSynchronous (REST/gRPC)Asynchronous (Messaging)
CouplingTighter - caller needs the callee to be up and responsive right nowLooser - producer doesn't need consumer to be available at the same instant
LatencyCaller waits for the full round tripCaller can continue immediately (fire-and-forget or eventual reply)
ResilienceA slow/down callee directly stalls/fails the caller (needs Circuit Breaker/Timeout)A down consumer just means messages queue up until it recovers
Best forRequests that genuinely need an immediate answer (e.g. "is this in stock right now?")Workflows that can tolerate eventual processing (e.g. "send a confirmation email")

gRPC vs REST: gRPC uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers (binary, strongly typed, code-generated clients/servers), which is typically faster and more bandwidth-efficient than JSON-over-REST, at the cost of being less human-readable/debuggable and less universally supported by simple tools like curl/browsers.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the key tradeoff between sync and async communication?Sync is simpler to reason about but couples the caller to the callee's availability/latency right now; async is more resilient/decoupled but adds eventual-consistency complexity
Why might gRPC be chosen over REST between internal services?Faster/more compact binary serialization (Protocol Buffers) and strongly-typed generated clients, at the cost of human-readability and universal tool support

topics.name: Service Registry and Discovery

beginner.content:
Why You Can't Just Hardcode a URL

In a microservices system running on containers/cloud infrastructure, service instances come and go - they scale up/down, restart, and get new IP addresses constantly. Hardcoding http://192.168.1.5:8081 for the Order Service simply breaks the moment that instance restarts elsewhere.

The Fix: Service Registry and Discovery

• A service registry is a directory where every service instance registers itself on startup ("I am Order Service, running at this address") and deregisters on shutdown.
• Service discovery is how a caller finds a live instance of the service it needs, by asking the registry instead of using a hardcoded address.
• Client-side discovery - the calling service queries the registry itself and picks an instance (possible load-balancing client-side).
• Server-side discovery - the caller talks to a load balancer/router, which queries the registry on the caller's behalf.

expert.content:
Netflix Eureka - A Concrete Example

Spring Cloud Netflix Eureka is a widely-used service registry in the Spring ecosystem.
codeExamples:
# Eureka Server - application.yml
server:
  port: 8761
eureka:
  client:
    register-with-eureka: false
    fetch-registry: false

# Order Service (a Eureka Client) - application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
eureka:
  client:
    service-url:
      defaultZone: http://localhost:8761/eureka/

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is hardcoding service URLs a problem in microservices?Instances scale/restart/move constantly in containerized environments, so a fixed IP:port breaks as soon as the instance changes
Client-side vs server-side discovery?Client-side: the caller queries the registry itself and picks an instance. Server-side: the caller talks to a load balancer that queries the registry on its behalf
What does Eureka provide in the Spring ecosystem?A service registry that services register with on startup and query to find live instances of other services by logical name

For a deeper dive specifically framed as a design pattern (including client-side vs server-side tradeoffs in more depth), see "Service Discovery Pattern" in the Microservices Design Patterns course.

topics.name: API Composition

beginner.content:
Combining Data From Multiple Services

A single screen in a client app (e.g. an order-detail page) often needs data that lives across several services - order details from Order Service, item info from Catalog Service, shipping status from Shipping Service. API Composition is the practice of combining results from multiple service calls into one response for the client.

Two Ways to Compose

• Client-side composition - the client itself calls each service separately and merges the results (simple, but chatty over the network and exposes internal service boundaries to the client).
• API Gateway-side composition - a single gateway/aggregator service calls all the needed backend services and returns one combined response to the client (client makes just one call; see the "API Gateway Pattern" and "Aggregator Pattern" in the Microservices Design Patterns course for the deeper pattern treatment).

expert.content:
The N+1 Problem Across Services

A subtle trap: composing a list of items where each item then requires its OWN follow-up call to another service (e.g. fetch 20 orders, then call Catalog Service once PER order to get item names) results in 1 + 20 = 21 network calls instead of 2. This "N+1" problem, familiar from ORMs, is even more expensive across a network than within a single database.

Mitigations

• Batch endpoints - ask the Catalog Service for many item IDs in one call instead of one call per item.
• Caching frequently-composed, slow-changing data.
• Denormalizing some data into the composing service if the read pattern justifies it (accepting some duplication for read performance).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is API composition?Combining results from multiple backend service calls into one response for the client
Client-side vs gateway-side composition?Client-side: the client itself calls each service and merges results. Gateway-side: one gateway/aggregator does the calling and merging, client makes one call
What is the N+1 problem in a microservices context?Composing a list where each item requires its own follow-up service call, multiplying network calls (1 list call + N per-item calls) - fixed by batch endpoints or caching

topics.name: Containerization with Docker

beginner.content:
Why Containers Matter for Microservices

With dozens of independently deployable services, each potentially needing a different runtime/dependency version, running them all directly on a shared host becomes unmanageable ("works on my machine" multiplied by N services). Containers solve this by packaging a service together with everything it needs (JVM, libraries, config) into one portable, isolated unit.

What Docker Gives You

• Consistent runtime - the exact same container image runs identically on a developer's laptop, in CI, and in production.
• Isolation - each container has its own filesystem/process space, so services don't fight over dependency versions.
• Fast startup - containers start in seconds, much faster than provisioning a full VM, which matters for scaling up quickly under load.
A Minimal Dockerfile for a Spring Boot Service
codeExamples:
# Dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/order-service-0.0.1.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8081
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

# Build and run
docker build -t order-service:1.0 .
docker run -p 8081:8081 order-service:1.0

# The service is now reachable at http://localhost:8081

expert.content:
Multi-Service Local Development with Docker Compose

Running several services (and their dependencies like a database) by hand quickly becomes tedious. Docker Compose lets you define and start a whole multi-container setup with one command.
codeExamples:
# docker-compose.yml
version: "3.8"
services:
  order-service:
    build: ./order-service
    ports:
      - "8081:8081"
    depends_on:
      - order-db

  order-db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: orders
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"

  inventory-service:
    build: ./inventory-service
    ports:
      - "8083:8083"

# Start everything defined above
docker compose up

# Illustrative: requires the referenced service directories/Dockerfiles
# to exist; shown to demonstrate multi-service local orchestration,
# not as a standalone runnable snippet.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why are containers a natural fit for microservices?They package each service with its exact runtime/dependencies into a portable, isolated unit that runs identically everywhere and starts in seconds
What problem does Docker Compose solve?Defining and starting a whole multi-service (+ dependencies like a DB) local setup with one command, instead of manually running each container
What's the difference between a Docker image and a container?An image is the packaged, immutable blueprint (filesystem + config); a container is a running instance of that image

topics.name: Container Orchestration with Kubernetes

beginner.content:
Why Do You Need an Orchestrator Beyond Plain Docker?

Docker packages and runs a single container, but running dozens of microservices in production raises questions Docker alone doesn't answer:

• Scaling - if traffic spikes, who starts more container instances?
• Self-healing - if a container crashes, who restarts it?
• Rolling updates - how do you deploy a new version with zero downtime?
• Service networking - how do containers on different hosts find each other?

Kubernetes (K8s) is a container orchestration platform that answers all of these - it schedules containers across a cluster of machines, restarts failed ones, scales them up/down, and load-balances traffic between them.

Core Kubernetes Concepts

ConceptWhat It Is
PodThe smallest deployable unit - one or more tightly-coupled containers sharing network/storage
DeploymentManages a set of identical Pod replicas, handles rolling updates and self-healing
ServiceA stable network endpoint (IP/DNS name) that load-balances traffic across a Deployment's Pods, even as Pods come and go
NamespaceA virtual cluster-within-a-cluster, used to separate environments/teams (e.g. dev, staging, prod)

Pods are ephemeral - they can be killed and recreated with a new IP address at any time. This is exactly why a stable Service abstraction sits in front of them.

A Minimal Deployment + Service for a Spring Boot App

This YAML manifest runs 3 replicas of a Spring Boot microservice and exposes them through a stable Service:
codeExamples:
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          image: myregistry/order-service:1.0.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
---
# service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: order-service
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  type: ClusterIP
# NOTE: illustrative Kubernetes manifest, not a runnable Java program

beginner.content:
Basic kubectl Commands

kubectl is the CLI used to interact with a Kubernetes cluster:
codeExamples:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml       # create/update resources from a manifest
kubectl get pods                       # list running pods
kubectl get deployments
kubectl scale deployment order-service --replicas=5   # manually scale
kubectl logs <pod-name>                # view a pod's logs
kubectl delete pod <pod-name>          # delete a pod (Deployment recreates it automatically)
# NOTE: shell commands, not Java - illustrative, no fabricated program output

expert.content:
How Kubernetes Achieves Self-Healing and Zero-Downtime Deploys

• A Deployment's controller loop constantly compares the desired replica count against the actual running Pods, and creates/deletes Pods to reconcile any difference - this is what makes a crashed Pod get automatically replaced.
• A rolling update replaces old Pods with new ones a few at a time (controlled by maxSurge/maxUnavailable), never taking all replicas down at once - this is how zero-downtime deploys work under the hood.
• Readiness probes tell Kubernetes when a Pod is actually ready to receive traffic (not just "started") - Spring Boot Actuator's /actuator/health/readiness endpoint is the standard hook for this.
• Liveness probes tell Kubernetes when a Pod is unhealthy and should be killed/restarted - distinct from readiness, since a Pod can be "alive" but temporarily not ready (e.g. still warming up a cache).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the difference between a Pod and a Deployment?A Pod is a single running instance of one or more containers; a Deployment manages a desired number of identical Pod replicas and handles their lifecycle (scaling, updates, healing)
Why does a Service exist if Pods already have IPs?Pod IPs change every time a Pod is recreated; a Service provides a stable, unchanging address that always routes to whichever Pods are currently healthy
Liveness probe vs readiness probe?Liveness answers "should this Pod be restarted?"; readiness answers "should this Pod currently receive traffic?" - a Pod can be alive but not ready

topics.name: Distributed Data Management in Microservices

beginner.content:
The Database-Per-Service Principle

In a microservices architecture, each service owns its own database, and no other service is allowed to access it directly - all access goes through that service's API.

Order Service --owns--> Order DB
Inventory Service --owns--> Inventory DB
Payment Service --owns--> Payment DB

Order Service does NOT query Inventory DB directly.
It calls the Inventory Service's API instead.

If services shared one database, changing a table's schema in one service could silently break every other service reading from it - this defeats the entire point of independent deployability.

The Challenges This Creates

• No cross-service SQL joins - you can't JOIN orders WITH inventory across two databases, so a request needing combined data must call multiple services and merge the results in application code (see the API Composition topic).
• Eventual consistency - since each service commits to its own database independently, there's no single ACID transaction spanning services; data becomes consistent across services after some delay, not instantly.
• Distributed transactions - a business operation like "place an order" might need to update Order, Inventory, and Payment data together; a classic two-phase-commit transaction across databases doesn't scale well in this world.

expert.content:
How This Is Actually Solved in Practice

The standard solutions to distributed data challenges are covered in full depth in the Microservices Design Patterns course - this topic gives the conceptual framing, not the implementation detail:

• Saga Pattern - coordinating a multi-service transaction as a sequence of local transactions with compensating rollback actions on failure.
• CQRS - separating the read model from the write model, often letting reads be served from a denormalized view built specifically to avoid needing cross-service joins.
• Event Sourcing - storing state as an event log, which naturally supports building multiple read-optimized views across service boundaries.

The mental shift required: distributed systems trade the comfortable guarantees of a single ACID database for independent scalability and deployability - accepting eventual consistency is usually the price paid.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why can't two microservices share one database?Sharing a database recreates tight coupling through the schema - any change to a shared table risks breaking every service that reads it, defeating independent deployability
How do you query data that spans two services?Call each owning service's API and combine the results in application code (API Composition), or maintain a denormalized read view built for that purpose (CQRS)
What does "eventual consistency" mean here?Data across services becomes consistent after some propagation delay, rather than instantly within one atomic transaction, since each service commits independently to its own database

topics.name: Microservices Security

beginner.content:
Two Different Trust Boundaries to Secure

Microservices security has two distinct concerns:

• Client → API Gateway - authenticating and authorizing an external user/client hitting your system's public entry point.
• Service → Service - authenticating calls between your own internal services, so a compromised or rogue service can't freely call every other service.

   External Client
         |
     [OAuth2 / JWT]
         v
    API Gateway  ---centralized auth check happens here---
         |
     [mTLS / internal token]
         v
   Order Service --calls--> Inventory Service

OAuth2 and JWT for Client Authentication

• A client authenticates once (e.g. via username/password or an identity provider) and receives a JWT (JSON Web Token) - a signed, self-contained token carrying claims about who the user is and what they're allowed to do.
• The client sends this JWT on every subsequent request (typically in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header).
• Because the JWT is signed, any service can verify it's genuine without calling back to a central auth server on every request - it just checks the signature.

The API Gateway as the Natural Auth Chokepoint

Rather than every single microservice re-implementing token validation, it's common to validate authentication once at the API Gateway and pass a trusted identity downstream (e.g. as a header), keeping individual services simpler. This is a direct extension of the API Gateway pattern already covered in the Microservices Design Patterns course.

expert.content:
Securing Service-to-Service Calls: mTLS and Service Mesh

Client-facing auth (OAuth2/JWT) doesn't automatically secure the internal network between your own services - if an attacker gets inside the cluster network, unencrypted/unauthenticated service-to-service calls are wide open.

• mTLS (mutual TLS) - both sides of a service-to-service call present a certificate, so each service can cryptographically verify who's actually calling it, not just encrypt the traffic.
• Rolling out mTLS by hand across every service is painful - this is one of the main reasons a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) exists: it injects a sidecar proxy next to every service that handles mTLS transparently, without changing application code.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is a signed JWT useful for microservices?Any service can verify it independently by checking the signature, without a round-trip call to a central auth server on every request
Why isn't client authentication enough to secure a microservices system?It only secures the boundary between the external client and the API Gateway; internal service-to-service calls need their own trust mechanism (e.g. mTLS)
What problem does a service mesh solve for security?It transparently provides mTLS and identity between services via sidecar proxies, without requiring every service to implement that logic itself

topics.name: Testing Microservices

beginner.content:
The Testing Pyramid, Adapted for Microservices

          /\
         /E2E\        <- few, slow, brittle, expensive
        /------\
       /Contract\      <- verify services agree without full deployment
      /----------\
     /Integration \    <- test a service against real dependencies (DB, etc.)
    /--------------\
   /   Unit Tests   \  <- many, fast, cheap, test logic in isolation
  /------------------\
The shape stays the same as traditional testing (lots of fast unit tests, fewer slow end-to-end tests), but microservices add a layer traditional monoliths don't need: contract testing.

Unit and Integration Tests

• Unit tests - test a single class/method's logic in isolation, mocking out dependencies. Fast, run on every commit.
• Integration tests - test a service against its real dependencies (an actual test database, e.g. via Testcontainers), verifying the service's own code + its direct infrastructure work together correctly.

Why Full End-to-End Tests Don't Scale Well

An end-to-end test that spins up every microservice in the system to verify one user flow is: slow (many services to boot), brittle (any one service being flaky fails the whole test), and hard to debug (a failure could be in any of a dozen services). The practical answer is to minimize how many of these you rely on and lean on contract testing instead for verifying inter-service compatibility.

expert.content:
Contract Testing

Contract testing (e.g. using the Pact framework) verifies that a service ("consumer") and the service it calls ("provider") agree on the shape of their API contract - without actually running both services together.

The flow: the consumer team writes a test defining what it expects from the provider's response; this generates a "contract" file; the provider team then runs that contract against their own service in CI to verify they still satisfy it. If the provider changes its API in a breaking way, the contract test fails in the provider's own pipeline - long before a real integration bug reaches production.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why are full end-to-end tests risky to rely on heavily in microservices?They're slow to run, brittle (any dependent service's flakiness fails the test), and hard to debug since a failure could originate in any of many services
What does contract testing verify that integration testing doesn't?That two independently-deployed services still agree on their API contract, without needing to actually run both together
Where does a Pact-style contract test run?The consumer generates the contract; the provider replays and verifies it against their own service independently in their own CI pipeline

topics.name: Microservices Deployment Strategies

beginner.content:
Rolling Deployment

Replaces old-version instances with new-version instances gradually, a few at a time, so the service never has zero running instances.

[v1][v1][v1][v1]   start: 4 old instances
[v2][v1][v1][v1]   replace one at a time...
[v2][v2][v1][v1]
[v2][v2][v2][v1]
[v2][v2][v2][v2]   done: all new
This is Kubernetes' default Deployment update strategy. Low infrastructure cost, but if v2 has a bug, some real users hit it before you notice and roll back.

Blue-Green Deployment

Run two complete environments - "blue" (current live version) and "green" (new version) - side by side. Once green is fully tested, switch all traffic to it at once (usually by repointing a load balancer/router).

• Rollback is instant - just switch traffic back to blue.
• Costs roughly 2x the infrastructure while both environments exist.

Canary Deployment

Route a small percentage of real traffic (e.g. 5%) to the new version while the rest keeps hitting the old version, then gradually increase the percentage as confidence grows.

• Limits the "blast radius" of a bad release to a small fraction of users.
• Requires good monitoring to actually detect problems in that 5% before rolling further.

expert.content:
Comparing the Three Strategies

StrategyDowntime RiskInfra CostRollback SpeedK8s Primitive
RollingLowLow (no duplicate env)Slow (roll forward/back gradually)Deployment (default strategy)
Blue-GreenVery lowHigh (2x during switch)Instant (repoint traffic)Two Deployments + Service switch
CanaryVery lowModerateFast (shift traffic weight back)Service mesh traffic splitting, or Ingress weight rules

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the main tradeoff of blue-green deployment?Very fast, safe rollback since it's just a traffic switch, but at the cost of running two full environments simultaneously
Why is canary deployment considered lower-risk than rolling?It exposes the new version to only a small, controlled percentage of real traffic first, limiting how many users are affected if there's a problem, before rolling out further

topics.name: The Twelve-Factor App

beginner.content:
What Is the Twelve-Factor App?

The Twelve-Factor App is a methodology (originating from Heroku) describing best practices for building software-as-a-service applications that are portable, scalable, and suited to modern cloud/container deployment - it's a foundational influence on how cloud-native and microservices applications are designed today.

The 12 Factors, Briefly

#FactorIdea
1CodebaseOne codebase tracked in version control, many deploys
2DependenciesExplicitly declare and isolate dependencies (no relying on system-wide packages)
3ConfigStore config in the environment, not in code
4Backing ServicesTreat databases/queues/etc. as attached resources, swappable via config
5Build, Release, RunStrictly separate the build, release, and run stages
6ProcessesExecute the app as one or more stateless processes
7Port BindingExport services via port binding, not relying on a runtime-injected web server
8ConcurrencyScale out via the process model (run more instances), not by making one process bigger
9DisposabilityFast startup and graceful shutdown maximize robustness
10Dev/Prod ParityKeep development, staging, and production as similar as possible
11LogsTreat logs as event streams, don't manage log files yourself
12Admin ProcessesRun admin/management tasks as one-off processes in the same environment

expert.content:
Why This Methodology Underpins Cloud-Native Design

• Factor 3 (Config) is exactly the Externalized Configuration Pattern covered in the Cloud-Native Patterns course - Spring Boot's application.yml + environment-variable overrides is a direct, practical implementation of this factor.
• Factor 6 (stateless processes) is precisely why Kubernetes can freely kill and recreate Pods without losing anything important - state belongs in a backing service (a database), never in the process's own memory.
• Factor 9 (disposability) directly maps to Kubernetes' readiness/liveness probes and rolling deployments - a service that can't start/stop quickly and cleanly breaks orchestration.
• Factor 11 (logs as event streams) is the reasoning behind centralized logging (ELK/EFK) rather than services managing their own log files on disk, which vanish the moment a container is destroyed.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does the Twelve-Factor App insist on statelessness?Stateless processes can be freely killed, restarted, and scaled by an orchestrator without any risk of losing data, since all real state lives in a backing service
How does Factor 3 (Config) relate to a container image?The same built container image should be deployable to dev/staging/prod unchanged - only its externally-injected configuration differs between environments

topics.name: Monitoring and Observability Fundamentals

beginner.content:
Why Observability Matters More in Microservices

In a monolith, a slow request means looking in one place - the monolith's own logs and stack traces. In a microservices system, a single user request might pass through a dozen services before returning a response - if it's slow or fails, which service is actually responsible?

Client -> API Gateway -> Order Service -> Inventory Service -> Payment Service -> ...
                                              ^
                              which one is actually slow? without observability, you're guessing.

The Three Pillars of Observability

PillarAnswersExample Tooling
LogsWhat exactly happened, in detail, at a point in time?ELK/EFK stack
MetricsHow is the system behaving in aggregate, over time? (latency, error rate, throughput)Prometheus + Grafana
TracesWhat path did one specific request take across services, and where did time go?Spring Cloud Sleuth, Zipkin, Jaeger

These three pillars are covered in much greater practical depth as Centralized Logging and Distributed Tracing in the Cloud-Native Patterns course - this topic exists to tie them together conceptually as one overall observability strategy, not to duplicate that depth.

expert.content:
Logs, Metrics, and Traces Are Complementary, Not Redundant

A typical debugging flow uses all three together: a metric dashboard shows latency spiked at 2:15pm → a trace for a slow request in that window shows most of the time was spent in the Inventory Service call → the Inventory Service's logs at that exact timestamp reveal it was retrying a failed database connection.

None of the three alone tells the full story - metrics tell you something is wrong and roughly when, traces tell you where in the call chain, and logs tell you why.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is observability a bigger deal for microservices than monoliths?A single request in a monolith stays in one process, but in microservices it crosses many services - you need dedicated tooling (traces) just to see the path a request took
What's the difference between a metric and a trace?A metric is an aggregate number over time (e.g. average latency across all requests); a trace follows one specific request's journey across every service it touched

topics.name: Introduction, Monolith vs Microservices, Advantages and Disadvantages

beginner.content:
What are microservices?

• A microservices architecture builds an application as a set of small, autonomous services, each around a business capability, owning its own data, independently deployable and communicating over the network (HTTP/REST, gRPC, messaging). Teams own services end to end ("you build it, you run it").
• A monolith is one deployable unit with one codebase and (usually) one database. A modular monolith keeps one deployment but enforces module boundaries: often the best starting point.
• Microservices are an organisational and architectural choice: they trade local complexity (a big codebase) for distributed-systems complexity (network, consistency, operations).
codeExamples:
Monolith                                   Microservices
+--------------------------+               +-------+  +-------+  +--------+
| UI | Catalogue | Orders  |               | Course|  | Order |  | Payment|
| Users | Payments | ...   |  --split-->   | svc   |  | svc   |  | svc    |
+--------------------------+               +---+---+  +---+---+  +---+----+
        one process                              |         |          |
        one database                          [DB-1]    [DB-2]     [DB-3]    (database per service)
        one deployment                       independent build, deploy, scale, team

intermediate.content:
Monolithic vs microservices

AspectMonolithMicroservices
DeploymentAll or nothingPer service, independent
ScalingScale the whole appScale only the hot service
TechnologyOne stackPolyglot possible (keep it limited)
DataOne shared database, ACID transactionsDatabase per service, eventual consistency
FailureOne bug can take everything downFailures isolated (if resilient design)
TeamLarge team, shared codeSmall autonomous teams per service
ComplexityCode complexityOperations complexity: network, discovery, tracing, versioning
LatencyIn-process callsNetwork calls (ms), partial failures
TestingEnd-to-end is simpleContract and integration testing needed
Best forSmall teams, early products, simple domainsLarge systems, many teams, different scaling needs

expert.content:
Advantages and disadvantages

• Advantages: independent deployment and release cadence, targeted scaling, fault isolation, technology freedom, smaller codebases that are easier to understand, team autonomy, easier replacement/rewrite of a single service.
• Disadvantages: distributed-system complexity (latency, partial failure, retries, timeouts), data consistency without cross-service transactions, operational overhead (CI/CD per service, monitoring, tracing, container orchestration), testing difficulty, versioning and compatibility, duplicated cross-cutting code, higher infrastructure cost, the need for DevOps maturity.
• When NOT to use them: a small team, an unclear domain, no automation. The common failure is a distributed monolith: services that must be deployed together, share a database or call each other synchronously in long chains. Start with a modular monolith and extract services when a boundary proves stable and a real need (scale, team autonomy) appears.
codeExamples:
Signs of a distributed monolith (anti-pattern)
 - services share one database / schema
 - a change needs coordinated releases of 3 services
 - synchronous call chains A -> B -> C -> D for one user request (latency multiplies, availability = product of all)
 - no one can run a service without the others

Availability maths: 4 services chained synchronously, each 99.9% available
   0.999^4 = 99.6% (about 35 hours of downtime per year instead of 8.7)

interviewQA: Monolith vs microservices: when to choose which?

Monolith (preferably modular) for small teams, new products and simple domains; microservices when a large organisation needs independent deployment, scaling and team autonomy and has the DevOps maturity to run distributed systems.
What are the main drawbacks of microservices?

Distributed-system complexity (network failures, latency), data consistency without ACID across services, operational overhead (deployment, monitoring, tracing), harder testing and versioning, and higher infrastructure cost.
What is a distributed monolith?
A system split into services that are still tightly coupled (shared database, coordinated deployments, long synchronous call chains), giving the downsides of both architectures.

topics.name: Architecture Patterns, Service Decomposition, DDD, Bounded Context and Database per Service

beginner.content:
Service decomposition

• How to split a system: by business capability (catalogue, ordering, payment, shipping) or by subdomain (DDD). Not by technical layer (a "database service", a "UI service") and not too fine-grained (nano-services).
• Good service boundaries: high cohesion (things that change together live together), loose coupling (few, stable interactions), single owning team, own data, can be explained in a sentence, can be deployed alone. Conway's law: system design mirrors communication structure: design teams and services together.
• Strangler fig migrates a monolith step by step. Event storming workshops reveal events, commands and aggregates that suggest boundaries.
codeExamples:
JavaSchoolLab domain split (by business capability)
 identity-service     users, registration, login, roles
 catalogue-service    courses, modules, topics, search
 learning-service     progress, bookmarks, streaks, notes
 assessment-service   quizzes, attempts, scoring, certificates
 payment-service      orders, invoices, payment gateway
 notification-service e-mail, push, in-app notifications
 analytics-service    events, dashboards (read model)

Rule of thumb: one service = one team = one database = one reason to change

intermediate.content:
Domain-Driven Design and bounded contexts

• DDD models software around the business domain with a ubiquitous language shared by developers and domain experts. Strategic design: split the domain into subdomains (core, supporting, generic) and bounded contexts.
• A bounded context is a boundary inside which a model and its language are consistent. The same word means different things in different contexts: a Customer in Billing (payment terms) is not the Customer in Support (tickets). A bounded context is the natural boundary of a microservice.
• Tactical design inside a context: entities (identity), value objects (immutable, equality by value), aggregates (consistency boundary with a root; one transaction modifies one aggregate), repositories, domain services, domain events. Context mapping describes relationships: shared kernel, customer/supplier, conformist, anti-corruption layer, open host service / published language.

expert.content:
Database per service

• Each service owns its data; no other service reads or writes its tables. Others use its API or events. Benefits: loose coupling, independent schema evolution, the freedom to pick the right store (PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch: polyglot persistence), independent scaling. Costs: no joins across services, no distributed ACID transactions (use sagas), data duplication and eventual consistency.
• Levels of separation: private tables in a shared DB (weak), schema per service (pragmatic), database per service (strong). Never share tables.
• Queries across services: API composition (aggregate calls), CQRS read models / materialized views fed by events, or a search/analytics store.
• Reference data: store ids (courseId) plus a small local copy of what you need (title) updated via events: avoid synchronous lookups on every read.

interviewQA: What is a bounded context and how does it relate to microservices?
A boundary within which a domain model and its language are consistent. Each bounded context is a natural candidate for a microservice with its own model and data.
Why database per service?

It decouples services (independent schema changes and technology choices) and enforces access through APIs or events; the cost is no joins or ACID transactions across services, handled with sagas, events and read models.
How do you decide service boundaries?

By business capability/subdomain and bounded context: high cohesion, loose coupling, single owning team, own data and independent deployability; avoid splitting by technical layer or into nano-services.

topics.name: Communication Overview and the Twelve-Factor App

beginner.content:
Communication styles at a glance

StyleExamplesUse forRisks
Synchronous request/responseREST/HTTP, gRPC, GraphQLQueries, commands needing an immediate answerTemporal coupling, cascading failures, latency chains
Asynchronous messagingKafka, RabbitMQ, SQSEvents, long work, decoupling, load levellingEventual consistency, ordering, duplicates, harder debugging
StreamingKafka Streams, WebSocket, SSEReal-time feeds, analyticsOperational complexity
• Rule: prefer asynchronous events between services for integration and keep synchronous calls short, few and protected by timeouts, retries and circuit breakers. Details in the Communication section.

intermediate.content:
The Twelve-Factor App

#FactorIn practice (Spring Boot / containers)
1CodebaseOne repo per service (or monorepo with clear modules), many deploys
2DependenciesDeclared in pom.xml/Gradle; no reliance on system libs
3ConfigEnvironment variables / Config Server / ConfigMaps, not in code
4Backing servicesDB, broker, cache are attached resources via URLs/credentials
5Build, release, runImmutable images; CI builds, CD releases, runtime runs
6ProcessesStateless processes; state in DB/cache (sessions in Redis/JWT)
7Port bindingEmbedded Tomcat/Netty exposes a port
8ConcurrencyScale out with more instances (HPA)
9DisposabilityFast startup, graceful shutdown (server.shutdown=graceful)
10Dev/prod paritySame backing services in dev (Testcontainers, Docker Compose)
11LogsWrite to stdout as an event stream; the platform aggregates
12Admin processesOne-off tasks as jobs (Flyway migration, batch) using the same image

expert.content:
Twelve-factor in a Spring Boot service

• Add modern extensions ("beyond twelve-factor"): API first (OpenAPI contract), telemetry (metrics, traces), authentication and authorisation from day one, health endpoints for orchestrators.
• Concretely: externalise everything environment-specific, never bake secrets into images, log JSON to stdout, handle SIGTERM (graceful shutdown), keep instances stateless, and make startup quick (lazy init, spring.main.lazy-initialization carefully, or native image/CRaC where needed).
codeExamples:
# application.yml : twelve-factor friendly
server:
  port: ${PORT:8080}                       # port binding
  shutdown: graceful                       # disposability
spring:
  lifecycle: { timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s }
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL}                         # config from the environment (backing service)
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
management:
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,prometheus
  endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true     # /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness for Kubernetes
logging.structured.format.console: ecs     # JSON logs to stdout (Spring Boot 3.4+)

interviewQA: What are the twelve-factor app principles?

A set of guidelines for cloud-native services: one codebase, declared dependencies, config in the environment, backing services as resources, separate build/release/run, stateless processes, port binding, scale out, disposability, dev/prod parity, logs as streams and admin tasks as one-off processes.
Why must microservices be stateless?
So any instance can serve any request and instances can be added, removed or restarted freely for scaling and resilience; state belongs in databases, caches or tokens.
Sync vs async communication?

Synchronous calls give an immediate answer but couple availability and latency; asynchronous messaging decouples services and absorbs load but brings eventual consistency, ordering and duplicate-handling concerns.

topics.name: Spring Boot Fundamentals, Creating Microservices, REST APIs, Layered Architecture and DTO Mapping

beginner.content:
Creating a microservice with Spring Boot

• Spring Boot provides auto-configuration, starters, an embedded server and production features (Actuator) so a service is a small executable jar. Generate from start.spring.io: spring-boot-starter-web, -validation, -data-jpa, -actuator, driver, lombok, mapstruct; Java 21, Maven/Gradle.
• One service = one Maven module = one deployable jar/container image. Keep small and focused, with a package structure by feature. Use virtual threads on Java 21 (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) for blocking I/O-heavy services.

intermediate.content:
REST API development and layered architecture

• REST conventions: nouns for resources (/api/v1/courses/{id}/modules), HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), status codes (200, 201 + Location, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429, 500, 503), pagination (?page=&size=), filtering/sorting, idempotent PUT/DELETE, HATEOAS optionally, OpenAPI docs with springdoc-openapi.
• Layers: controller (HTTP, validation, mapping: thin) → service (business logic, transactions) → repository (persistence) → database; plus DTOs/mappers, entities, clients (calls to other services), config. Controllers never touch repositories; services never touch HttpServletRequest. Alternative: hexagonal (ports/adapters) for complex domains.

expert.content:
DTO and entity mapping

• Never expose entities across the API boundary: use DTOs (Java records) for requests/responses. Reasons: API stability independent of the schema, no lazy-loading/N+1 during serialisation, no mass assignment (clients setting role/price), different shapes per use case.
• Map with MapStruct (compile-time, fast, type-safe) or hand-written mappers. Keep separate DTOs for create/update/response; versioned DTO packages for API versions. Between services, DTOs are the published contract: evolve them compatibly (add optional fields, never remove/rename without versioning).

interviewQA: Why use DTOs instead of entities in REST APIs?
DTOs decouple the API from the persistence model, prevent lazy-loading and recursion issues, stop mass assignment and allow different representations per use case and versions of the contract.
What is the role of each layer in a Spring Boot microservice?
Controller handles HTTP and validation; service holds business logic and transactions; repository handles persistence; DTO/mapper types shape data at the boundary; client classes call other services.
Which status code does a successful POST creating a resource return?
201 Created with a Location header for the new resource (200 is possible but less precise); 204 for deletes without a body.

topics.name: Configuration Management, Externalized Configuration and Spring Profiles

beginner.content:
Externalized configuration

• Spring Boot reads config from many sources in a defined precedence (highest wins): command line args → SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON → OS environment variables → application-{profile}.yml → application.yml → defaults in code. Relaxed binding: env var SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL maps to spring.datasource.url.
• Rule: the same build artifact runs in every environment; only configuration changes (twelve-factor). Secrets never live in the repo or the image.
• Bind typed groups with @ConfigurationProperties (validated, immutable records) instead of scattered @Value.

intermediate.content:
Spring profiles

• Profiles group beans and properties per environment: application-dev.yml, application-prod.yml; activate with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod (env var) or --spring.profiles.active=prod. @Profile("dev") on beans/configuration; profile groups (spring.profiles.group.prod=prod,metrics); spring.config.import to include optional files.
• Typical split: dev (H2/Testcontainers, debug logging, mocks of other services), test, staging, prod (real DB, JSON logs, tracing sampling). Keep the differences small: large per-profile differences mean untested production paths.
codeExamples:
# application.yml (shared)
spring.application.name: learning-service
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,prometheus

---
spring.config.activate.on-profile: dev
spring.datasource.url: jdbc:h2:mem:learning
logging.level.com.javaschoollab: DEBUG
jsl.clients.catalogue.url: http://localhost:8081

---
spring.config.activate.on-profile: prod
spring.datasource.url: ${DB_URL}
jsl.clients.catalogue.url: http://catalogue-service            # resolved by DNS / Kubernetes Service
logging.level.root: INFO

@Configuration
@Profile("dev")
class DevDataLoader { @Bean CommandLineRunner seed(CourseRepository r) { return args -> r.save(new Course("Demo")); } }

expert.content:
Configuration management across many services

• With dozens of services you need a central, versioned, auditable way to manage config: Spring Cloud Config Server (Git-backed), Kubernetes ConfigMaps/Secrets (often mounted as env vars/files), HashiCorp Vault or cloud secret managers for secrets, Consul KV.
• Practices: config in Git (reviewed, rollback), per-environment overrides, encrypt secrets ({cipher} in Config Server, Sealed Secrets/External Secrets in Kubernetes), refresh without restart where safe (@RefreshScope, Spring Cloud Bus), validate config at startup (fail fast with @Validated properties), and use feature flags (Unleash, FF4J, Togglz, LaunchDarkly) for runtime toggles instead of redeploying.

interviewQA: What is the order of precedence for Spring Boot configuration?
Roughly: command-line arguments, environment variables, profile-specific files, application files, defaults; higher sources override lower ones, which lets the same artifact run in any environment.
Why use @ConfigurationProperties instead of @Value?
It binds a group of properties to a typed, validated, ideally immutable object, giving type safety, IDE metadata, relaxed binding and one place to see all settings of a feature.
How do you handle secrets in microservices?
Never in code or images: inject from a secret store (Vault, cloud secret manager, Kubernetes Secrets with encryption/External Secrets), restrict access, rotate and avoid logging them.

topics.name: Validation, Global Exception Handling, Logging and API Versioning

beginner.content:
Validation

• Use Jakarta Bean Validation (spring-boot-starter-validation): annotate DTOs (@NotBlank, @Size, @Email, @Min, @Positive, @Pattern, @Valid for nesting), trigger with @Valid @RequestBody, validate path/query params with @Validated on the class and constraints on parameters. Custom constraints (@ValidSlug) for domain rules; cross-field via class-level constraints.
• Validate at the edge (controller) for format, and in the domain for business invariants. Fail with 400/422 and field-level messages. Never trust data from other services either (defensive consumers).

intermediate.content:
Global exception handling (RFC 9457 Problem Details)

• Centralise error mapping with @RestControllerAdvice. Return a consistent error body: Spring 6 supports Problem Details (ProblemDetail, RFC 9457: type, title, status, detail, instance + extensions) with spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true.
• Map: validation → 400/422 with field errors; not found → 404; conflicts/duplicates/optimistic lock → 409; auth → 401/403; downstream failures → 502/503/504; unexpected → 500 with a correlation/trace id and no stack trace or SQL in the body. Log once with the cause at the right level (4xx warn/info, 5xx error).

expert.content:
Logging and API versioning

• Logging: SLF4J + Logback (default) or Log4j2; log to stdout in JSON (Spring Boot 3.4 structured logging: logging.structured.format.console=ecs|gelf|logstash), include traceId/spanId/correlation id (Micrometer Tracing adds them to MDC), service name and environment. Levels: ERROR (needs action), WARN (unexpected but handled), INFO (business events), DEBUG (off in prod). Never log secrets, tokens, full card numbers or personal data; use parameterised messages (log.info("enrolled {}", id)); do not log and rethrow the same exception at every layer.
• API versioning: services must evolve without breaking consumers. Strategies: URI (/api/v1/..., simplest and most common), header (Accept: application/vnd.jsl.v2+json), query param. Spring Framework 7 adds first-class versioning support. Rules: additive changes are non-breaking (new optional fields/endpoints); removing/renaming/changing types is breaking: introduce v2, run both, deprecate (Deprecation/Sunset headers), then retire. Consumers use the tolerant reader pattern; test compatibility with contract tests.

interviewQA: How do you handle exceptions globally in Spring Boot?

With @RestControllerAdvice (and ResponseEntityExceptionHandler) mapping exceptions to consistent HTTP status codes and RFC 9457 Problem Details bodies, including a trace id, without leaking internals.
What makes an API change breaking?

Removing or renaming fields/endpoints, changing types or semantics, or making optional input required. Adding optional fields or endpoints is compatible; breaking changes need a new version and a deprecation period.
What should and should not be logged?
Log business events, errors with context, trace/correlation ids in structured form; never log secrets, tokens, passwords or sensitive personal data, and avoid duplicated log-and-rethrow noise.

topics.name: Synchronous vs Asynchronous, REST Communication, RestClient, WebClient and OpenFeign

beginner.content:
Synchronous REST between services

• In synchronous communication the caller waits for the response (REST/HTTP+JSON, gRPC). Simple and familiar, good for queries and commands that need an answer, but it creates temporal coupling: if the callee is slow or down, the caller suffers. Availability of a chain multiplies; latency adds.
• Always apply: timeouts (connect + read), retries for idempotent calls with backoff, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and fallbacks; propagate trace/correlation ids and the caller's identity (JWT). Prefer coarse-grained calls over chatty ones; avoid long chains.

intermediate.content:
RestClient (Spring 6.1+) and WebClient

• RestClient is the modern synchronous, fluent HTTP client (replaces RestTemplate, which is in maintenance mode). Works great with virtual threads. Build with RestClient.builder() (inject RestClient.Builder so Boot adds observability/trace headers), set base URL and defaults, use retrieve().body(Type.class) and onStatus for error mapping.
• WebClient (Spring WebFlux) is the reactive, non-blocking client: returns Mono/Flux; use for streaming, high concurrency with few threads, or reactive stacks. Do not call .block() inside a reactive pipeline.
• HTTP Interface clients (@HttpExchange) generate a typed client from an interface on top of RestClient/WebClient: Spring's own "Feign".

expert.content:
OpenFeign (Spring Cloud OpenFeign)

• OpenFeign is a declarative REST client: write an interface with Spring MVC annotations, Spring Cloud generates the implementation, integrates with service discovery (name = "catalogue-service" resolved via LoadBalancer), Resilience4j, interceptors (auth/trace headers), encoders/decoders and error decoders.
• Configure timeouts (spring.cloud.openfeign.client.config.default.connect-timeout/read-timeout), logging, retries (disable Feign's own retryer and use Resilience4j to avoid double retries), and a custom ErrorDecoder mapping 4xx/5xx to domain exceptions. Add @EnableFeignClients. Keep clients thin and DTOs in the consumer (or a published client library with the contract).

interviewQA: RestTemplate vs RestClient vs WebClient vs Feign?

RestTemplate is legacy blocking; RestClient is the modern fluent blocking client (good with virtual threads); WebClient is reactive and non-blocking; OpenFeign is a declarative interface-based client integrated with discovery and Resilience4j. Choose by stack and style.
Why are timeouts mandatory on service calls?

Without them a slow dependency makes threads wait indefinitely, exhausting thread/connection pools and causing cascading failures; timeouts bound the damage and let retries and circuit breakers react.
What is temporal coupling?
When a service can only work if another is available right now, because it waits synchronously for it. Asynchronous messaging removes this coupling.

topics.name: Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, Event-Driven Architecture and Message Serialization

beginner.content:
Event-driven architecture

• Services communicate through events: immutable facts about something that happened (OrderPlaced, CourseCompleted). The producer publishes without knowing the consumers; consumers react independently. Benefits: loose coupling, scalability, resilience (the consumer can be down; messages wait), easy addition of new consumers, audit trail and real-time reactions.
• Kinds of messages: event (fact, past tense, many consumers), command (request to do something, one consumer), document/query-reply. Event styles: event notification (small, consumer calls back for details), event-carried state transfer (carries the data; no callbacks), event sourcing (events are the source of truth).
• Costs: eventual consistency, ordering and duplicate delivery to handle, harder debugging, schema evolution: invest in tracing, idempotent consumers and schema registries.
codeExamples:
Producer (order-service)            Broker (Kafka topic "orders.events")           Consumers
 OrderPlaced  ----------------->  [ partition 0 | partition 1 | partition 2 ]  -->  payment-service (group "payment")
                                                                               -->  notification-service (group "notify")
                                                                               -->  analytics-service (group "analytics")
 Each consumer GROUP gets every event once; instances inside a group share partitions (scale-out)

intermediate.content:
Apache Kafka with Spring Boot

• Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log. Concepts: topic, partition (unit of parallelism and ordering: order is guaranteed per partition), key (same key → same partition → ordered per entity, e.g. orderId), offset, consumer group (each partition consumed by one member), replication factor, retention (events stay for days: replay!), log compaction.
• Producer settings for safety: acks=all, enable.idempotence=true, retries; consumer: manual/after-processing commit, idempotent processing, dead-letter topic (DLT) with DefaultErrorHandler/@RetryableTopic. Delivery guarantee is at-least-once by default; exactly-once only within Kafka (transactions) or via idempotent consumers.

expert.content:
RabbitMQ and message serialization

• RabbitMQ is a message broker (AMQP) with exchanges (direct, topic, fanout, headers) routing to queues via binding keys; consumers ack messages (removed once acknowledged). Great for task queues, work distribution, complex routing, request/reply, priority and per-message TTL. Kafka is a log for high-throughput streams, replay and many independent consumer groups; RabbitMQ is a smart broker for routing and queue semantics. Spring: spring-boot-starter-amqp, RabbitTemplate, @RabbitListener, dead-letter exchanges, publisher confirms, manual acks.
• Serialization: JSON (readable, flexible), Avro/Protobuf with a Schema Registry (compact, typed, enforced compatibility: backward/forward/full). Rules: never remove or change a field's meaning; add optional fields with defaults; include event id, type, version, occurredAt, correlation id in an envelope; use type headers carefully (avoid Java class names across services: they couple consumers to producer packages).

interviewQA: Kafka vs RabbitMQ?

Kafka is a partitioned replicated log for high-throughput streaming, replay and multiple independent consumer groups; RabbitMQ is a routing broker with queues and acknowledgements, suited to work queues, flexible routing and request/reply.
How does Kafka guarantee ordering?
Only within a partition. Using the entity id as the message key sends all events of that entity to the same partition, preserving their order.
How do you evolve event schemas safely?
Use a schema registry with compatibility rules, only add optional fields with defaults, never remove or repurpose fields, version events, and keep consumers tolerant of unknown fields.

topics.name: Timeouts, Retries, Idempotency and Distributed Messaging

beginner.content:
Timeouts and retries

• Timeout budget: choose timeouts from the user-visible SLA downwards: if the API must answer in 2 s and calls 2 services, each gets well under 1 s. A timeout must be shorter than the caller's own timeout, otherwise the caller gives up while work continues. Set connect and read timeouts; HTTP clients default to infinite.
• Retries help with transient failures (network blips, deployments, 503), but only for idempotent operations (GET, PUT, DELETE, or POST with an idempotency key). Use exponential backoff with jitter and a small max attempts; never retry non-transient errors (400/401/403/404/422). Beware retry amplification: three layers each retrying 3 times = 27 calls (retry storm). Retry at one layer and give a retry budget.
codeExamples:
# Resilience4j retry with exponential backoff and jitter (retry only what is transient)
resilience4j.retry.instances.payment:
  max-attempts: 3
  wait-duration: 200ms
  enable-exponential-backoff: true
  exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2
  enable-randomized-wait: true               # jitter spreads retries
  retry-exceptions: [java.net.SocketTimeoutException, org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException]
  ignore-exceptions: [com.javaschoollab.BadRequestException]

// Timeout budget: user -> gateway (2s) -> order-service (1.5s) -> payment-service (800ms)
// Each hop's timeout is smaller than its caller's.

intermediate.content:
Idempotency

• An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. Needed because networks and brokers deliver at-least-once and clients retry. Naturally idempotent: PUT /users/5 {...}, DELETE, setting a value. Not idempotent: POST /payments, "increment counter", "send e-mail".
• Idempotency key pattern: the client sends a unique Idempotency-Key (UUID) header; the server stores key → response (or status) in a table with a unique constraint and, if the key repeats, returns the stored result instead of re-executing. For consumers: store processed message ids (inbox table) or make the write itself idempotent (upsert, unique business key, conditional update).

expert.content:
Distributed messaging concerns

• Delivery semantics: at-most-once (may lose), at-least-once (default; duplicates possible → idempotent consumers), exactly-once (end to end is a myth; achieved by at-least-once + idempotency, or Kafka transactions inside Kafka).
• Ordering: only within a partition/queue; design so that unrelated events do not depend on order, or key by entity. Poison messages: a message that always fails blocks the partition: use limited retries + dead-letter queue/topic + alerting + a replay tool.
• Backpressure and consumer lag (monitor!), batching, outbox for atomic "DB write + publish", inbox for deduplication, request/reply over messaging with correlation ids when really needed, message TTL for time-sensitive commands.

interviewQA: Why must consumers be idempotent?
Brokers deliver at-least-once and retries or rebalances can redeliver messages; idempotent processing (inbox table, unique keys, upserts) ensures duplicates do not cause duplicate side effects.
What is a retry storm and how do you prevent it?

Layers of clients each retrying failed calls multiply load on an already struggling service. Prevent with retries at one layer, exponential backoff with jitter, limited attempts, circuit breakers and retry budgets.
What is an idempotency key?
A client-generated unique id sent with a request so the server can detect repeats and return the original result instead of executing the operation twice.

subTopics.name: Phase 4 · Service Discovery and API Gateway (Core)

topics.name: Service Discovery: Netflix Eureka and Consul

beginner.content:
Why service discovery?

• In dynamic environments (containers, autoscaling) instances start, stop and change IP/port constantly: hard-coded URLs do not work. Service discovery lets services register themselves and clients look up healthy instances by logical name (catalogue-service).
• Client-side discovery: the client queries a registry and load-balances itself (Eureka + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, Consul). Server-side discovery: a router/load balancer does it (Kubernetes Service/kube-proxy, AWS ALB, Ingress): the client calls a stable DNS name.
• On Kubernetes you usually do not need Eureka: Services + DNS (http://catalogue-service) provide discovery and load balancing. Use Eureka/Consul on VMs, hybrid setups, or when you need metadata-based routing.
codeExamples:
Client-side discovery (Eureka)                       Server-side discovery (Kubernetes)
 order-service                                         order-service
   | 1. "where is catalogue-service?"                     | calls http://catalogue-service  (stable DNS)
   v                                                      v
 [Eureka registry] -> instances: 10.0.1.5:8081, 10.0.1.6:8081
   | 2. client picks one (round robin)                  [K8s Service] -> kube-proxy -> pod 1 / pod 2 / pod 3

intermediate.content:
Netflix Eureka

• Eureka Server is the registry (spring-cloud-starter-netflix-eureka-server, @EnableEurekaServer). Eureka Client services register on startup with their name, host, port and health URL, send heartbeats (every 30 s) and are evicted if heartbeats stop (90 s). Clients cache the registry locally and refresh periodically (30 s): discovery keeps working if Eureka is briefly down, but data can be stale.
• Self-preservation mode: if many instances stop heartbeating at once (network partition), Eureka stops evicting to avoid wiping the registry: it favours availability over consistency (AP in CAP).
• Run several Eureka peers (peer replication) in production; secure the registry (Spring Security basic/mTLS); tune lease and refresh intervals for faster failure detection; register with the Actuator health check (eureka.client.healthcheck.enabled=true).

expert.content:
Consul and how Eureka works internally

• HashiCorp Consul: service registry + health checks (HTTP/TCP/script, agents on each node) + key-value store (config) + DNS interface + service mesh (mTLS, intents/ACLs). Consistent via Raft (CP for the catalog), with gossip between agents. Spring: spring-cloud-starter-consul-discovery, -config.
EurekaConsulKubernetes DNS
ModelAP registry, client cacheCP catalog + health agentsPlatform built-in
HealthHeartbeats (+ optional health check)Rich active checksReadiness probes
ExtrasSpring-centricKV, mesh, multi-DCServices, Ingress
UseVMs/Spring CloudPolyglot, hybrid, meshDefault on Kubernetes
• How Eureka works: register → heartbeat renew → server replicates to peers → clients fetch the full/delta registry and cache it → LoadBalancer chooses an instance → eviction when the lease expires.

interviewQA: How does Eureka work?

Services register with the Eureka server and renew a lease with heartbeats; the server evicts instances whose lease expires and replicates the registry to peers. Clients fetch and cache the registry and pick instances with a client-side load balancer.
What is Eureka self-preservation mode?
When many heartbeats are missed at once Eureka assumes a network problem and stops evicting instances, trading consistency for availability so a partition does not empty the registry.
Do you need Eureka on Kubernetes?
Usually no: Kubernetes Services and DNS provide discovery and load balancing. Eureka or Consul still make sense on VMs, in hybrid environments or when you need extra metadata or mesh features.

topics.name: API Gateway, Spring Cloud Gateway, Routing, Rate Limiting and Request Filtering

beginner.content:
What is an API gateway?

• An API gateway is the single entry point for clients. It handles cross-cutting concerns once: routing to services, authentication (validate JWT), rate limiting, TLS termination, CORS, request/response transformation, logging/tracing, caching, and sometimes API composition or protocol translation. It hides internal topology: clients call api.javaschoollab.com/courses, not ten services.
• Variants: one gateway for all, or Backend for Frontend (a gateway per client type: web, mobile). Risks: single point of failure/bottleneck (run several, keep it stateless), business logic creeping in (keep it thin), extra latency.
• Options: Spring Cloud Gateway (WebFlux or the newer MVC variant), Kong, NGINX, Envoy, AWS API Gateway, Kubernetes Ingress/Gateway API.
codeExamples:
Client (web / mobile)
      |
      v
 [ API Gateway ]  -> TLS, JWT validation, rate limit, CORS, routing, tracing headers
      |--> /api/identity/**    -> identity-service
      |--> /api/courses/**     -> catalogue-service   (lb://catalogue-service)
      |--> /api/learning/**    -> learning-service
      '--> /api/payments/**    -> payment-service

intermediate.content:
Spring Cloud Gateway: routes, predicates and filters

• A route = id + target URI (lb://service uses discovery + LoadBalancer, or an HTTP URL) + predicates (when to match: Path, Method, Header, Host, Query, After, Weight) + filters (modify request/response: StripPrefix, RewritePath, AddRequestHeader, CircuitBreaker, Retry, RequestRateLimiter, DedupeResponseHeader). Global filters apply to all routes (auth, logging, correlation id).
• Define routes in YAML or Java DSL; add spring-cloud-starter-gateway (reactive) and the discovery client.
codeExamples:
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      default-filters:
        - DedupeResponseHeader=Access-Control-Allow-Origin
        - AddResponseHeader=X-Content-Type-Options, nosniff
      routes:
        - id: catalogue
          uri: lb://catalogue-service
          predicates: [ Path=/api/courses/** ]
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=0
            - name: CircuitBreaker
              args: { name: catalogueCb, fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/courses }
            - name: Retry
              args: { retries: 2, statuses: BAD_GATEWAY,SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, methods: GET, backoff: { firstBackoff: 100ms, maxBackoff: 1s, factor: 2 } }
        - id: payments
          uri: lb://payment-service
          predicates: [ Path=/api/payments/** , Method=POST,GET ]
          filters: [ name: RequestRateLimiter, args: { redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10, redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20, key-resolver: "#{@userKeyResolver}" } ]

// Java DSL
@Bean RouteLocator routes(RouteLocatorBuilder b) {
    return b.routes().route("learning", r -> r.path("/api/learning/**").filters(f -> f.addRequestHeader("X-Gateway", "jsl")).uri("lb://learning-service")).build();
}

expert.content:
Rate limiting, request filtering and gateway security

• Rate limiting protects services from abuse and overload: algorithms token bucket (burst + steady rate; used by the Redis rate limiter), leaky bucket, fixed/sliding window. Key by user id, API key or IP (KeyResolver); respond 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After. Spring Cloud Gateway's RequestRateLimiter needs Redis (shared counters across gateway instances).
• Request filtering: a global filter to validate the JWT and forward claims as headers, add a correlation id, enforce size limits, block bad paths/IPs, strip internal headers coming from clients (never trust client-supplied X-User-Id), log access. Order matters (Ordered).
• Gateway security: terminate TLS, validate tokens (resource server), CORS config in one place, security headers, WAF in front. Still verify authorisation in each service (zero trust): the gateway is not the only gate.

interviewQA: What is an API gateway and what does it do?

The single entry point to the system that routes requests to services and centralises cross-cutting concerns: authentication, rate limiting, TLS, CORS, logging/tracing, resilience filters and sometimes composition.
What are routes, predicates and filters in Spring Cloud Gateway?
A route maps matching requests (predicates such as Path or Header) to a target URI and applies filters that modify the request/response (StripPrefix, Retry, CircuitBreaker, rate limiter).
Why is the gateway not enough for security?

It is one layer; internal services can also be reached from inside the network. Each service must validate tokens and enforce authorisation (zero trust), and gateway-added headers must not be trusted from clients.

topics.name: Load Balancing: Client-Side vs Server-Side

beginner.content:
Load balancing concepts

• A load balancer distributes requests across instances for scalability, availability (skip unhealthy instances) and even utilisation. Algorithms: round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, least response time, random, IP/consistent hashing (stickiness for caches), zone-aware.
