• Server-side (L4/L7): a dedicated component in front: NGINX, HAProxy, AWS ALB/NLB, Kubernetes Service/Ingress, Envoy. Clients know one address. Client-side: the client holds the instance list (from discovery) and picks an instance itself: Spring Cloud LoadBalancer. No extra hop, no central bottleneck, but logic lives in every client.
• Health: only route to ready instances (readiness probes/health checks); drain connections on shutdown.
Client-side (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer)Server-side (Nginx, ALB, K8s Service)
WhereInside the calling serviceSeparate network component
Instance listFrom discovery (Eureka/Consul) cached in the clientManaged by the balancer / platform
Extra hopNoYes
Language couplingLibrary per languageLanguage agnostic
Smart routingEasy (zone, metadata, hints)Depends on the product
Typical useService-to-service on Spring CloudEdge traffic, Kubernetes, polyglot

intermediate.content:
Spring Cloud LoadBalancer

• Replaces Netflix Ribbon. Annotate a RestClient.Builder/WebClient.Builder with @LoadBalanced (Feign uses it automatically) and call http://service-name/...: LoadBalancer resolves the name through the DiscoveryClient (Eureka/Consul/Kubernetes) and chooses an instance: default round robin; RandomLoadBalancer, weighted, zone-preference, same-instance preference, request-based sticky session, health-check filtering (spring.cloud.loadbalancer.configurations=health-check).
• Configure per client with a @LoadBalancerClient(name = "...", configuration = ...); enable retry on the next instance carefully (only idempotent), cache instance lists (spring.cloud.loadbalancer.cache).

expert.content:
Load balancing on Kubernetes and in front of the cluster

• Kubernetes Service (ClusterIP) load-balances across ready pods (kube-proxy iptables/IPVS, round robin-ish, connection-level). Gotcha: HTTP/2 and gRPC use long-lived connections, so all requests stick to one pod: use a client-side/headless-service balancer, a service mesh (Envoy/Istio/Linkerd) or L7 balancing.
• Ingress / Gateway API (NGINX, Traefik, Envoy Gateway) load-balances external HTTP traffic; a cloud LoadBalancer Service provisions an ALB/NLB. Use readiness probes so traffic reaches only ready pods and preStop + graceful shutdown so in-flight requests finish.
• Also consider geographic/DNS load balancing (Route 53, Cloudflare), global failover, and session affinity only when unavoidable (prefer stateless services).
codeExamples:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: catalogue-service }
spec:
  selector: { app: catalogue }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 8081 } ]         # callers use http://catalogue-service (DNS), balanced over ready pods
---
# headless service: DNS returns every pod IP for client-side balancing (gRPC)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: catalogue-headless }
spec: { clusterIP: None, selector: { app: catalogue }, ports: [ { port: 8081 } ] }

# Spring Cloud Kubernetes discovery uses the K8s API instead of Eureka
# spring.cloud.kubernetes.discovery.enabled=true

interviewQA: Client-side vs server-side load balancing?

Client-side: the caller gets the instance list from discovery and picks an instance (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer), with no extra hop. Server-side: a separate balancer (NGINX, ALB, Kubernetes Service) fronts the instances and clients call one address.
Which algorithms do load balancers use?

Round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, least response time, random, and hash-based (IP/consistent hashing) for stickiness, usually combined with health checks to skip unhealthy instances.
Why can gRPC traffic be unbalanced on Kubernetes?
gRPC/HTTP2 keeps long-lived connections, and the Service balances per connection, so one pod receives most requests. Use client-side balancing with a headless service or an L7 proxy/service mesh.

topics.name: Spring Cloud Config Server, Centralized Configuration, Refresh and Spring Cloud Bus

beginner.content:
Spring Cloud Config Server

• Config Server serves configuration over HTTP from a backend, typically a Git repository (versioned, auditable, rollback via commits). Clients fetch {application}/{profile}/{label} at startup. Add spring-cloud-config-server, @EnableConfigServer, set spring.cloud.config.server.git.uri. Backends: Git, Vault, JDBC, filesystem, S3.
• Layout in the config repo: application.yml (shared), catalogue-service.yml, catalogue-service-prod.yml. Precedence: profile-specific over application-specific over shared.
• Secure it: authentication, TLS, encrypt secrets ({cipher}..., symmetric/asymmetric keys) or integrate Vault; do not expose it publicly; run 2+ instances and let clients cache/fail-fast with retry.
codeExamples:
// config-server
@SpringBootApplication @EnableConfigServer
public class ConfigServerApplication { public static void main(String[] a) { SpringApplication.run(ConfigServerApplication.class, a); } }

# config-server application.yml
server.port: 8888
spring.cloud.config.server.git:
  uri: https://github.com/javaschoollab/config-repo
  default-label: main
  search-paths: '{application}'
  clone-on-start: true
  username: ${GIT_USER}
  password: ${GIT_TOKEN}
encrypt.key: ${CONFIG_ENCRYPT_KEY}                 # symmetric key for {cipher} values

# config-repo/catalogue-service-prod.yml
spring.datasource.url: jdbc:postgresql://catalogue-db:5432/catalogue
spring.datasource.password: '{cipher}AQBb3...'       # encrypted: curl -X POST config-server/encrypt -d 'plain'

# client
spring:
  application.name: catalogue-service
  config.import: "configserver:http://config-server:8888"
  cloud.config: { fail-fast: true, retry: { max-attempts: 6 } }

intermediate.content:
Distributed configuration refresh

• By default config is read at startup. To change it without redeploying use @RefreshScope beans and POST /actuator/refresh (expose refresh): scoped beans are re-created with new values. @ConfigurationProperties beans rebind on refresh automatically. Not everything is refreshable (datasource pools, server port): restart for those.
• Refreshing N instances manually does not scale: use Spring Cloud Bus: all instances subscribe to a broker topic (RabbitMQ/Kafka); one POST /actuator/busrefresh (or a Git webhook to Config Server's /monitor) broadcasts the change event; every instance refreshes. In Kubernetes prefer ConfigMaps with a rolling restart (or Spring Cloud Kubernetes config reload, Reloader).

expert.content:
Centralized configuration: Config Server vs Kubernetes ConfigMaps vs Vault

Spring Cloud ConfigK8s ConfigMap/SecretVault / cloud secrets
StoreGit, JDBC, VaultCluster API objects (etcd)Dedicated secret store
VersioningGit historyGitOps (Argo CD/Flux)Secret versions
Refresh@RefreshScope, BusRestart or reloaderLease/dynamic secrets, agent sidecar
Best forSpring-centric estates, VMsKubernetes-native configCredentials, certificates, rotation
• Principles: separate config from code, per-environment overrides, secrets encrypted and access-controlled, audit changes, validate on startup, avoid a single point of failure (HA + local caches), and keep the amount of dynamic config small: every refreshable property is a production behaviour change without a deployment.
codeExamples:
# GitOps for Kubernetes config: config changes are pull requests applied by Argo CD
# repo: environments/prod/catalogue/configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: catalogue-config }
data:
  JSL_PRICING_DISCOUNT_PERCENT: "10"
  SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod

# Vault dynamic database credentials (short-lived)
spring:
  config.import: "vault://"
  cloud.vault: { uri: https://vault:8200, authentication: KUBERNETES, kv.enabled: true, database: { enabled: true, role: catalogue } }

interviewQA: What problem does Spring Cloud Config solve?

Centralised, versioned and environment-aware configuration for many services, served from Git (or Vault), so config is managed in one place, can be audited and rolled back, and secrets can be encrypted.
How do you refresh configuration without restarting services?

Use @RefreshScope beans with the /actuator/refresh endpoint, and Spring Cloud Bus (/actuator/busrefresh) to broadcast the refresh to all instances; on Kubernetes use ConfigMap updates with rolling restarts or a reloader.
Why is it risky to make many properties refreshable at runtime?
Each refreshable value changes production behaviour without a deployment, review pipeline or rollout, so it needs strong governance, validation and auditing; keep dynamic config minimal.

topics.name: Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, CircuitBreaker Abstraction, Gateway/Eureka/Feign Recap and Spring Cloud Kubernetes

beginner.content:
Spring Cloud at a glance

ConcernSpring Cloud projectNotes
ConfigConfig Server / Config Client, Spring Cloud BusGit-backed, refresh
DiscoveryNetflix Eureka, Consul, Zookeeper, KubernetesRegistry or platform
RoutingSpring Cloud Gateway (reactive or MVC)Predicates, filters
Client callsOpenFeign, HTTP interfaces, LoadBalancerDeclarative + balancing
ResilienceSpring Cloud CircuitBreaker (Resilience4j)Abstraction over breakers
MessagingSpring Cloud Stream (Kafka/Rabbit binders), FunctionFunctional bindings
ObservabilityMicrometer Tracing (replaces Sleuth), ActuatorTraces and metrics
ContractsSpring Cloud ContractConsumer-driven contracts
KubernetesSpring Cloud KubernetesDiscovery/config from the K8s API
• Eureka, Gateway, OpenFeign and LoadBalancer were covered in the previous section; this lesson covers the abstraction layers and Kubernetes integration.

intermediate.content:
Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker abstraction

• Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker provides a vendor-neutral API (CircuitBreakerFactory/ReactiveCircuitBreakerFactory) with implementations for Resilience4j (recommended), Spring Retry and Sentinel. Use it programmatically (factory.create("id").run(supplier, fallback)), in Feign (spring.cloud.openfeign.circuitbreaker.enabled) and as a Gateway filter. Customise with Resilience4JCircuitBreakerFactory configurers. (Full Resilience4j usage in the Resilience section.)

expert.content:
Spring Cloud Kubernetes and when to drop components

• Spring Cloud Kubernetes lets Spring apps use Kubernetes as the platform: discovery via the K8s API (DiscoveryClient reading Services/Endpoints), config from ConfigMaps and Secrets as property sources (with optional reload on change), leader election, health indicators. Needs RBAC permissions (a ServiceAccount allowed to read services/endpoints/configmaps).
• Simplify on Kubernetes: use native Services + DNS instead of Eureka, ConfigMaps/Secrets instead of Config Server, Ingress/Gateway API (or keep Spring Cloud Gateway for app-level filters), K8s probes instead of Eureka heartbeats, a service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) for mTLS, retries and traffic shifting. Keep libraries for what the platform does not provide: Resilience4j, OpenFeign/HTTP interfaces, Micrometer, Spring Security.
codeExamples:
<!-- dependencies -->
<dependency><groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId><artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-kubernetes-client-all</artifactId></dependency>

# application.yml
spring:
  application.name: catalogue-service
  cloud.kubernetes:
    discovery.enabled: true
    config:   { enabled: true, name: catalogue-config, namespace: jsl }
    secrets:  { enabled: true, name: catalogue-secrets }
    reload:   { enabled: true, mode: event, strategy: refresh }       # refresh beans when the ConfigMap changes

# RBAC so the pod may read config and endpoints
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: { name: spring-cloud-k8s, namespace: jsl }
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps", "secrets", "services", "endpoints", "pods"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

interviewQA: What does Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker provide?

A common abstraction over circuit breaker libraries (Resilience4j, Spring Retry, Sentinel) with a factory API, plus integration with Feign and Gateway so you can add fallbacks and limits without tying code to one library.
What does Spring Cloud Kubernetes do?

It lets Spring applications use Kubernetes for service discovery (K8s API) and configuration (ConfigMaps/Secrets as property sources with reload), reducing the need for Eureka and Config Server on the platform.
Which Spring Cloud components can you drop on Kubernetes?
Eureka (use Services/DNS), Config Server (use ConfigMaps/Secrets/GitOps) and often the Ribbon-style balancing; keep Resilience4j, Feign/HTTP interfaces, Micrometer/OpenTelemetry and Spring Security.

topics.name: Circuit Breaker and Resilience4j

beginner.content:
The circuit breaker pattern

• Calls to a failing or slow dependency waste threads and make things worse (cascading failure). A circuit breaker wraps the call and tracks outcomes in a sliding window. States: CLOSED (normal; calls pass), OPEN (failure rate or slow-call rate above a threshold: calls fail fast without touching the dependency for a wait duration), HALF_OPEN (after the wait, a few trial calls are allowed: success closes the circuit, failure reopens it).
• Benefits: fail fast (protects threads and latency), gives the dependency time to recover, enables fallbacks (cached/default data), and surfaces a clear metric (state, failure rate).
codeExamples:
failure rate >= threshold
   CLOSED ----------------------------------> OPEN
     ^                                          |
     | trial calls succeed                      | wait duration elapsed
     |                                          v
     +<------------------------------------- HALF_OPEN
                   trial call fails -> back to OPEN

 CLOSED: calls flow, results recorded in a sliding window (count- or time-based)
 OPEN: calls rejected immediately (CallNotPermittedException) -> fallback
 HALF_OPEN: permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState trial calls decide

intermediate.content:
Resilience4j with Spring Boot

• Resilience4j is the lightweight, functional fault-tolerance library (successor of Netflix Hystrix): CircuitBreaker, Retry, TimeLimiter, Bulkhead, ThreadPoolBulkhead, RateLimiter, Cache. Spring Boot starter resilience4j-spring-boot3 + AOP; annotate methods (@CircuitBreaker, @Retry, @Bulkhead, @TimeLimiter, @RateLimiter) or use the Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker abstraction. Metrics via Micrometer; events via actuator.
• Key settings: slidingWindowType/Size, failureRateThreshold, slowCallDurationThreshold + slowCallRateThreshold, minimumNumberOfCalls, waitDurationInOpenState, permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState, recordExceptions/ignoreExceptions (do not count business errors like 404 as failures).
codeExamples:
# application.yml
resilience4j.circuitbreaker:
  instances:
    paymentService:
      sliding-window-type: COUNT_BASED
      sliding-window-size: 20
      minimum-number-of-calls: 10                    # do not judge before enough calls
      failure-rate-threshold: 50                     # open when >= 50% fail
      slow-call-duration-threshold: 2s
      slow-call-rate-threshold: 80                   # or when >= 80% are slower than 2s
      wait-duration-in-open-state: 20s
      permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 5
      automatic-transition-from-open-to-half-open-enabled: true
      record-exceptions: [java.io.IOException, java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException, org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException]
      ignore-exceptions: [com.javaschoollab.PaymentDeclinedException]       # a declined card is not a failure of the service

@Service
class PaymentGateway {
    @CircuitBreaker(name = "paymentService", fallbackMethod = "pending")
    PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest r) { return client.charge(r); }

    PaymentResult pending(PaymentRequest r, Throwable t) {               // same params + Throwable
        log.warn("payment service unavailable: {}", t.toString());
        return PaymentResult.queued(r.orderId());                        // degrade: accept the order, charge later
    }
}

expert.content:
Fallbacks, monitoring and tuning

• Fallback design: return a cached value, a default/empty result, a degraded feature (recommendations → popular courses), queue the work for later, or fail with a clear 503. A fallback must not call the same failing dependency, and must be fast and safe (no side effects that surprise users).
• Observe: expose /actuator/circuitbreakers, Micrometer metrics (resilience4j_circuitbreaker_state, ..._calls_seconds, failure rate) → Grafana panels and alerts when a breaker is OPEN. Log state transitions (registerEventConsumer).
• Tuning: window size large enough to be statistically meaningful; minimumNumberOfCalls to avoid opening on one error at low traffic; separate breakers per dependency (and per critical operation); combine with timeouts (a hung call counts as slow/failed only if a timeout cuts it); order of aspects (Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter ( Bulkhead ( Function ))))).

interviewQA: How does a circuit breaker work?

It monitors calls to a dependency. While CLOSED calls pass; when the failure or slow-call rate exceeds a threshold it OPENS and rejects calls immediately for a wait period; then HALF_OPEN allows trial calls to decide whether to close again.
Which exceptions should count as failures?
Technical failures (timeouts, connection errors, 5xx). Business or client errors (404, validation, a declined payment) should be ignored, otherwise valid business outcomes open the circuit.
What makes a good fallback?
A fast, side-effect-safe degraded result (cache, default, popular items, queued work) that does not depend on the failing service, with the degradation visible in logs and metrics.

topics.name: Retry, Timeout, Exponential Backoff and Retry Storm Prevention

beginner.content:
Retry and timeout patterns

• Retry repeats a failed call for transient faults. Conditions: operation idempotent; failure is transient (timeouts, connection reset, 502/503/504, 429 with Retry-After); small max attempts (2-3); backoff between attempts. Never retry 4xx client errors or non-idempotent POSTs without idempotency keys.
• Timeout (TimeLimiter, HTTP client timeouts) bounds how long you wait. Every remote call needs one; the value comes from the SLO, the callee's p99 and the caller's own timeout (callee < caller).
• Order: Retry wraps CircuitBreaker (retries consume the breaker's window and stop when it is open) which wraps the timeout.
codeExamples:
resilience4j:
  retry.instances.catalogue:
    max-attempts: 3
    wait-duration: 200ms
    enable-exponential-backoff: true
    exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2        # 200ms, 400ms
    enable-randomized-wait: true             # jitter
    randomized-wait-factor: 0.5
    retry-exceptions: [java.io.IOException, java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException, org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException$ServiceUnavailable]
    ignore-exceptions: [org.springframework.web.client.HttpClientErrorException]
  timelimiter.instances.catalogue:
    timeout-duration: 800ms
    cancel-running-future: true

@Retry(name = "catalogue")
@CircuitBreaker(name = "catalogue", fallbackMethod = "cached")
@TimeLimiter(name = "catalogue")
CompletableFuture<CourseDto> fetch(UUID id) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> client.get(id)); }

intermediate.content:
Exponential backoff with jitter

• Fixed delay retries from many clients arrive in waves and keep a recovering service down. Exponential backoff doubles the wait each attempt (100 ms, 200, 400, 800...) up to a cap; jitter randomises it so clients de-synchronise ("full jitter": random between 0 and the exponential cap, "decorrelated jitter").
• Honour the server: if it sends Retry-After or 429, wait at least that long. Cap total retry time under the caller's deadline (deadline propagation).

expert.content:
Retry storms and how to prevent them

• Retry storm / retry amplification: a dependency slows down; every layer retries; request volume multiplies (3 layers × 3 attempts = 27×), turning a brief slowdown into a prolonged outage.
• Prevention: (1) retry at one layer only (usually the closest to the failing call, or the edge); (2) retry budgets (cap retries to ~10% of requests, as in Envoy/gRPC); (3) exponential backoff + jitter; (4) circuit breaker so retries stop when the dependency is clearly down; (5) timeouts shorter than the caller's; (6) load shedding at the server (reject early with 429/503 when overloaded); (7) idempotency so retries are safe; (8) deadline propagation (pass the remaining time budget downstream so deeper layers stop working on abandoned requests).
• Test with fault injection (latency, errors) and watch request rates and queue depths.

interviewQA: What is exponential backoff with jitter?
Increasing the wait between retries exponentially (capped) and randomising it, so many clients do not retry in synchronised waves and the failing service gets time to recover.
What is a retry storm?

Layers of retries multiplying load on a struggling dependency, turning a brief slowdown into an outage. Prevent with single-layer retries, backoff and jitter, retry budgets, circuit breakers, timeouts and load shedding.
Which requests are safe to retry?
Idempotent operations (GET, PUT, DELETE) or requests carrying an idempotency key, and only for transient failures such as timeouts and 502/503/504; not 4xx errors.

topics.name: Bulkhead, Rate Limiting, Fallback Mechanism and Fault Isolation

beginner.content:
Bulkhead pattern

• Like ship bulkheads, a bulkhead isolates resources so one failing part cannot sink the rest. Without it, a slow dependency consumes all threads/connections of the service and every endpoint, including unrelated ones, hangs.
• Types: semaphore bulkhead (limit concurrent calls: maxConcurrentCalls, maxWaitDuration), thread-pool bulkhead (separate pool and queue per dependency), connection-pool partitioning (separate HTTP/DB pools per dependency), deployment bulkheads (separate service instances/queues for critical vs non-critical traffic), cell-based architecture.
• With Java 21 virtual threads thread exhaustion is rarer, but downstream connection and concurrency limits still matter: use semaphores.

intermediate.content:
Rate limiting (as a resilience tool)

• Rate limiting caps the request rate a client/tenant/service may make, protecting capacity and enforcing fairness. Applied at the edge (gateway: per user/API key/IP) and inside services (protect an expensive endpoint; Resilience4j RateLimiter: limitForPeriod, limitRefreshPeriod, timeoutDuration) and client-side (do not exceed a third-party API quota).
• Responses: 429 Too Many Requests + Retry-After and rate-limit headers (X-RateLimit-Remaining). Algorithms: token bucket, sliding window; distributed limiting needs a shared store (Redis). Combine with load shedding (drop low-priority work first) and priority queues.

expert.content:
Fallbacks and fault isolation

• Fallback mechanism = graceful degradation: when a dependency fails return something useful: cache (stale data with a flag), default/static content, reduced functionality (hide recommendations), alternate provider (secondary payment gateway), queue and process later (accept the order, charge when the gateway recovers), clear failure (503 with guidance) for critical operations where wrong data is worse than none (balances).
• Fault isolation techniques: bulkheads, circuit breakers, timeouts, asynchronous events instead of sync chains, separate databases/caches per service, per-tenant isolation (cell architecture), feature flags/kill switches to disable a failing feature, graceful degradation tiers, health-based routing and chaos engineering to prove the isolation works.
• Design question for every dependency: "what does the user see if this is down?"

interviewQA: What is the bulkhead pattern?

Isolating resources (thread pools, semaphores, connection pools, instances) per dependency or workload so that a failure or slowdown in one cannot exhaust the resources needed by the rest of the system.
How do you prevent cascading failures?

Use timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiting/load shedding, asynchronous communication instead of long synchronous chains, fallbacks and isolated data stores, and verify with fault-injection tests.
What is graceful degradation?
Continuing to serve a reduced but useful experience when a dependency fails (cached or default data, hidden optional features, queued work) instead of failing the whole request.

topics.name: Database per Service in Practice: Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, Migrations and Sharding

beginner.content:
Spring Data JPA and Hibernate per service

• Each service has its own schema/database, its own entities and repositories, and its own migrations. Use Spring Data JPA + Hibernate for aggregates, with the practices from the Hibernate course: LAZY associations, DTO projections, open-in-view=false, short transactions, @Version optimistic locking, batch fetching and query-count tests.
• No foreign keys across services: reference other aggregates by id (UUID courseId), not by entity association; integrity is eventual and enforced by events/sagas. Keep aggregates small (one transaction per aggregate).

intermediate.content:
Database migrations in a multi-service world

• Each service runs its own Flyway/Liquibase migrations on startup (or as a Kubernetes init container/Job for safer rollouts). Rules: versioned and immutable, reviewed, tested on production-like data; ddl-auto=validate.
• Zero-downtime changes with rolling deployments (old and new versions run together): use expand/contract: (1) expand: add nullable column/new table (compatible with the old code); (2) deploy new code writing both/reading new; (3) backfill; (4) contract: drop the old column in a later release. Avoid renames and type changes in one step; create indexes CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL); batch big backfills.
• Concurrent startup of N instances: Flyway uses a DB lock so only one migrates; prefer a dedicated migration job for big changes.
codeExamples:
# application.yml
spring:
  flyway:
    enabled: true
    locations: classpath:db/migration
    baseline-on-migrate: false
    validate-on-migrate: true

-- V7__expand_enrollment_status.sql  (safe with the old version still running)
ALTER TABLE enrollment ADD COLUMN completed_at TIMESTAMP NULL;
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_enrollment_student ON enrollment (student_id);        -- PostgreSQL: no table lock (cannot run in a transaction: flyway: executeInTransaction=false)

-- V8__backfill.sql (a later release, in batches)
UPDATE enrollment SET completed_at = updated_at WHERE status = 'COMPLETED' AND completed_at IS NULL;

# Kubernetes: run migrations once before the new pods start
# initContainers: [{ name: migrate, image: catalogue:2.4.0, args: ["--spring.main.web-application-type=none", "--flyway.only=true"] }]

expert.content:
Database sharding and scaling data

• Sharding splits one logical dataset across multiple databases (shards) by a shard key (tenantId, userId hash, region) to scale writes/storage beyond one node. Strategies: range (hot spots), hash/consistent hashing (even), directory/lookup (flexible), geographic. Costs: cross-shard queries/transactions are hard, re-sharding is painful, hot keys, operational load. Do it last.
• Scale in this order: indexes and query tuning → caching (Redis) → read replicas (CQRS reads, replication lag) → partitioning (table partitions) → vertical split (service per capability, already done) → sharding or a distributed SQL database (CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, Vitess, Citus).
• Choose the right store per service (polyglot persistence): relational for transactions, document/key-value for flexible/high-volume data, search (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch), time-series, cache.

interviewQA: Why should entities of different services not have foreign keys between them?
Each service owns its data; cross-service foreign keys couple schemas and deployments. Reference other aggregates by id and maintain consistency through events or sagas.
What is the expand/contract migration pattern?

Make schema changes in compatible steps: add new structures first (expand), deploy code that uses them and backfill data, and remove the old structures in a later release (contract), so old and new service versions run safely side by side.
When should you shard a database?
Only after exhausting indexing, caching, read replicas and partitioning, because sharding makes cross-shard queries, transactions and re-sharding complex.

topics.name: Distributed Transactions: 2PC, Saga, Choreography vs Orchestration and Eventual Consistency

beginner.content:
The problem and Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

• With database per service a business operation (place order: reserve stock, charge payment, create shipment) spans several databases: no single ACID transaction.
• 2PC: a coordinator asks all participants to prepare (lock and vote), then commit or abort. Provides atomicity (XA/JTA), but: blocking (locks held while waiting for the coordinator; a coordinator failure leaves participants stuck), latency, reduced availability (all must be up), and not supported by many brokers/NoSQL/SaaS. It also tightly couples services. Avoid 2PC in microservices; use sagas and eventual consistency.
codeExamples:
2PC                                            Saga
 coordinator                                    order-service: create order (PENDING)  -> commit local tx
   prepare -> payment DB, stock DB, order DB      -> payment-service: charge             -> commit local tx
   (all hold locks, wait)                         -> stock-service: reserve stock        -> commit local tx   (fails!)
   commit/abort                                   <- compensate: refund payment, cancel order (new local txs)
 atomic, but blocking, slow, brittle            eventually consistent, available, needs compensations

intermediate.content:
The Saga pattern

• A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each in one service and each publishing an event/message to trigger the next. If a step fails, compensating transactions undo the effects of the previous steps (semantic undo: refund, cancel, release). No distributed locks; data is eventually consistent.
• Design issues: compensations must be idempotent and retryable and cannot fail permanently; some actions are non-compensable (sent e-mail): order them last or use pivot transactions (point of no return); lack of isolation (other transactions see intermediate states: use semantic locks (PENDING status), commutative updates, re-reads, versioning); each step persists saga state.
codeExamples:
Place order saga (happy path and failure)
 1. order-service   : createOrder(PENDING)                     compensation: cancelOrder
 2. stock-service   : reserveStock                             compensation: releaseStock
 3. payment-service : chargeCustomer                           compensation: refund
 4. order-service   : approveOrder(CONFIRMED)

 failure at step 3 (card declined):
   payment-service -> PaymentFailed event
   stock-service   -> releaseStock (compensate step 2)
   order-service   -> cancelOrder / REJECTED (compensate step 1)

expert.content:
Choreography vs orchestration

ChoreographyOrchestration
ControlDecentralised: services react to each other's eventsA central orchestrator (saga coordinator) commands participants
CouplingLoose, but implicit flow (hard to see)Participants know the orchestrator's API; flow explicit
ComplexityFine for 2-4 steps; becomes a tangle with more (cyclic dependencies)Better for long/complex flows; one place to see and test
Failure handlingEach service emits failure eventsOrchestrator tracks state and triggers compensations
RiskHard to trace and changeOrchestrator can become a "god service"
ToolsKafka/RabbitMQ eventsTemporal, Camunda, Conductor, Axon, Step Functions, custom state machine
• Eventual consistency: replicas/services converge to a consistent state given time and no new updates. Design the UX for it: show pending states, use optimistic UI, notify on completion, make operations idempotent, and expose status endpoints. Define business-acceptable consistency windows (seconds, not days).

interviewQA: What is the Saga pattern?

A way to manage a business transaction across services as a sequence of local transactions, each triggering the next by events or commands, with compensating transactions to undo completed steps if a later step fails.
Choreography vs orchestration?

Choreography has services react to each other's events with no central controller (loose coupling, implicit flow); orchestration uses a central coordinator that directs each step and compensation (explicit flow, easier for complex sagas).
Why avoid 2PC in microservices?
It holds locks across services, reduces availability, adds latency, tightly couples participants and is unsupported by many modern stores and brokers; sagas with eventual consistency are preferred.

topics.name: Transactional Outbox and CQRS

beginner.content:
The dual-write problem and the transactional outbox

• A service must update its database and publish an event. Doing both separately is a dual write: if the DB commit succeeds but the broker publish fails (or vice versa) the system becomes inconsistent. You cannot make a DB and a broker atomic with a simple transaction.
• Transactional outbox: in the same local database transaction save the business change and insert the event into an outbox table. A separate relay reads unpublished rows and publishes them to the broker, then marks them published (at-least-once: consumers must be idempotent). Relay options: polling publisher (scheduled job, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), or CDC (Debezium reading the DB log: lower latency, no polling load, preserves order).

intermediate.content:
CQRS: separate reads and writes

• CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) uses different models for commands (writes: validate, enforce invariants, change state) and queries (reads: optimised, denormalised views). The write side emits events; projections update a read model (another table, Elasticsearch, Redis, a materialized view), often in another service. Result: fast, tailored queries, independent scaling of reads vs writes, and a way to join data across services without distributed queries.
• Cost: complexity and eventual consistency between write and read (the UI may not see its own write immediately: return the new state from the command, use version/polling or "read your writes" tricks). Do not use CQRS everywhere: apply it to areas with complex reads/high read load or cross-service views. Can be done simply: same DB with separate query classes/projections (no events).
• CQRS + Event Sourcing is a separate, optional step (state stored as events).

expert.content:
Outbox in production: CDC with Debezium, ordering and housekeeping

• Polling vs CDC: polling is simple but adds latency (the poll interval) and database load; Debezium (Kafka Connect) tails the database transaction log (WAL/binlog) and publishes each outbox insert to Kafka with low latency and preserved commit order; the outbox event router SMT routes rows to topics by aggregate_type and uses aggregate_id as the key. Delete or archive published rows (CDC reads the log, so a delete right after insert is fine).
• Guarantees: at-least-once (a relay crash after publishing and before marking leads to a duplicate): consumers must be idempotent (inbox). Ordering per aggregate is kept by keying on the aggregate id. Monitor outbox backlog (age of the oldest unpublished event) and alert on it; add an event id and schema version.
• The mirror image on the consumer side is the inbox pattern.
codeExamples:
{
  "name": "outbox-connector",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "database.hostname": "orders-db", "database.dbname": "orders", "topic.prefix": "orders",
    "table.include.list": "public.outbox_event",
    "transforms": "outbox",
    "transforms.outbox.type": "io.debezium.transforms.outbox.EventRouter",
    "transforms.outbox.table.field.event.id": "id",
    "transforms.outbox.table.field.event.key": "aggregate_id",
    "transforms.outbox.table.field.event.payload": "payload",
    "transforms.outbox.route.by.field": "aggregate_type",
    "transforms.outbox.route.topic.replacement": "${routedByValue}.events"
  }
}

-- housekeeping when polling: keep the table small
DELETE FROM outbox_event WHERE published_at < now() - interval '7 days';
-- alert: select extract(epoch from now() - min(created_at)) from outbox_event where published_at is null   (age of the oldest unpublished event)

interviewQA: What problem does the transactional outbox solve?

The dual-write problem: updating the database and publishing an event atomically. The event is stored in an outbox table in the same local transaction and relayed to the broker afterwards, giving at-least-once publication without distributed transactions.
What is CQRS and when is it useful?

Separating the write model (commands, invariants) from one or more read models optimised for queries, updated through events. Useful for complex or high-volume reads and for cross-service views, at the cost of eventual consistency and extra complexity.
How do you handle the eventual consistency of a CQRS read model in the UI?
Return the updated state from the command, show pending/optimistic UI, use version numbers or polling until the projection catches up, and keep the lag short and monitored.

topics.name: Spring Security, Authentication vs Authorization, JWT, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect

beginner.content:
Authentication vs authorization, and security in a microservice world

• Authentication (AuthN): who are you? Authorization (AuthZ): what may you do? In microservices, authentication happens once (at an identity provider / auth server) and the proof travels as a token; every service validates the token and authorises locally ("trust nobody": zero trust). Avoid per-service login forms and shared session stores.
• Architecture: Authorization Server / IdP (Keycloak, Spring Authorization Server, Okta, Auth0, Entra ID) issues tokens; the API gateway and services are OAuth2 resource servers; clients (SPA, mobile) use Authorization Code + PKCE; services use Client Credentials for service-to-service.
codeExamples:
Browser/mobile --(1) login: Authorization Code + PKCE--> Authorization Server (Keycloak)
              <--(2) access token (JWT) + id token + refresh token--
Browser --(3) Authorization: Bearer <access token>--> API Gateway --(4) forwards token--> catalogue-service
catalogue-service (resource server): verify signature (JWKS), issuer, audience, expiry -> read roles/scopes -> authorise

intermediate.content:
JWT and OAuth 2.0

• A JWT (header.payload.signature) carries claims: iss (issuer), sub (user), aud (audience), exp, iat, scope/roles. It is signed (RS256/ES256 with the IdP's private key; services verify with the public key from the JWKS endpoint), not encrypted: never put secrets in it. Short expiry (5-15 min) because JWTs cannot be revoked easily; use refresh tokens, token revocation lists/introspection for sensitive cases.
• OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework (delegated access) with grant types: Authorization Code + PKCE (users; the recommended flow), Client Credentials (machine-to-machine), Refresh Token; Implicit and Password grants are deprecated. Scopes describe the access requested (courses.read).
• OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer on OAuth 2.0: adds the ID token (a JWT about the authentication event: sub, email, name), the openid scope, the /userinfo endpoint and discovery (/.well-known/openid-configuration). OAuth = authorization, OIDC = authentication.

expert.content:
Common token pitfalls

• Validate everything: signature, iss, aud, exp/nbf (small clock skew), algorithm (reject none; pin expected algorithms). Never accept an unsigned token or decode without verifying. Do not use ID tokens as API access tokens; do not use access tokens as proof of login in clients.
• Token storage (browser clients): prefer a BFF (backend for frontend) holding tokens server-side with an HttpOnly session cookie; avoid localStorage (XSS). Mobile: secure storage.
• Revocation/logout: JWTs are valid until exp: keep them short, rotate refresh tokens, support opaque tokens + introspection where immediate revocation matters, and propagate logout events.
• Do not put authorisation data that changes often in the token (stale permissions): keep roles coarse in the token and check fine-grained rules against fresh data in the service.

interviewQA: OAuth 2.0 vs OpenID Connect?
OAuth 2.0 is a delegated-authorisation framework issuing access tokens for APIs; OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top (ID token, userinfo, discovery) to authenticate the user.
Why are JWT access tokens short-lived?
They are self-contained and valid until expiry, so they cannot be easily revoked; a short lifetime limits the damage of a leak, while refresh tokens renew sessions.
What must a resource server validate in a JWT?
The signature (against the issuer's JWKS), expected algorithm, issuer, audience, expiry/not-before, and then scopes/roles for authorisation; never trust a token without verification.

topics.name: API Gateway Security, Service-to-Service Authentication, RBAC and Method-Level Security

beginner.content:
Gateway security and zero trust

• The gateway terminates TLS, validates the token (or delegates to the IdP), applies rate limits, CORS and security headers, and may forward identity (the original JWT, or trusted headers it sets) downstream. Zero trust: internal services still validate the token and authorise; network location is not trust. Strip client-provided identity headers; do not let services be reachable bypassing the gateway (network policies).
• Token relay: the gateway passes the user's access token to services (TokenRelay filter) so authorisation uses the end user's identity; or token exchange (RFC 8693) to get a down-scoped token for a downstream audience.
codeExamples:
spring:
  cloud.gateway.routes:
    - id: learning
      uri: lb://learning-service
      predicates: [ Path=/api/learning/** ]
      filters:
        - TokenRelay=                              # forward the user's access token downstream
        - RemoveRequestHeader=X-User-Id            # never trust client-supplied identity headers

# Kubernetes NetworkPolicy: only the gateway may call learning-service
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: learning-allow-gateway }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: learning-service } }
  ingress: [ { from: [ { podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api-gateway } } } ], ports: [ { port: 8080 } ] } ]

intermediate.content:
Service-to-service authentication

• Options: (1) OAuth2 Client Credentials: the calling service gets its own short-lived token (scopes/roles for what it may do) from the auth server and sends it as a bearer token: simple, auditable, works across platforms. (2) Propagate the user's JWT (token relay) when the call is on behalf of the user. (3) mTLS: each service has a certificate; the mesh (Istio/Linkerd, SPIFFE/SPIRE) or app terminates mutual TLS: strong workload identity, automatic rotation, encrypts east-west traffic. (4) API keys/shared secrets: weak, avoid.
• Combine: mTLS for transport identity + JWT for end-user identity and authorisation. Cache client-credential tokens until near expiry.

expert.content:
Role-based access control and method-level security

• RBAC: users get roles (STUDENT, INSTRUCTOR, ADMIN) which grant permissions. Roles in the token (from the IdP) give coarse access; fine-grained rules (own resources, attributes) are checked in the service: ABAC/ownership checks. Principle of least privilege; deny by default.
• Method security (@EnableMethodSecurity): @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')"), @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_courses.write')"), SpEL with parameters and beans (@enrollmentSecurity.isOwner(#id, authentication)), @PostAuthorize (check the returned object), @PostFilter, @Secured. Enforce at the service layer so rules apply regardless of the entry point (REST, messaging, jobs).
• Test authorisation with @WithMockUser/jwt() request post-processors; include negative tests (403/404 for other users' data).

interviewQA: How do microservices authenticate each other?

Typically with OAuth2 client credentials (each service gets its own short-lived token) or mTLS from a service mesh for workload identity; end-user identity is propagated with the user's JWT (token relay or token exchange).
Why validate tokens in every service, not only at the gateway?
Zero trust: services can be reached from inside the network or via misconfiguration, so each must verify the token and authorise; the gateway is just one layer.
What does method-level security add?
Fine-grained authorisation rules (@PreAuthorize/@PostAuthorize with roles, scopes and ownership checks) enforced on service methods, independent of how they are invoked.

topics.name: HTTPS/TLS, Secrets Management and Keycloak Integration

beginner.content:
HTTPS and TLS

• Encrypt in transit everywhere: edge TLS at the gateway/ingress (public certificates, Let's Encrypt/cert-manager) and east-west TLS between services (mTLS via a service mesh, or Spring Boot SSL bundles). Use TLS 1.2+/1.3, strong ciphers, HSTS, redirect HTTP to HTTPS; automate certificate rotation. Terminate TLS at the ingress only if the internal network is trusted and policies enforce isolation; otherwise re-encrypt.
• Spring Boot 3.1+ SSL bundles (spring.ssl.bundle.pem.*/jks.*) configure keystores/truststores for server and clients with reload on change.
codeExamples:
# Spring Boot SSL bundle (PEM files mounted from a Kubernetes Secret / cert-manager)
spring:
  ssl.bundle.pem:
    server:
      keystore: { certificate: file:/certs/tls.crt, private-key: file:/certs/tls.key }
      truststore: { certificate: file:/certs/ca.crt }
      reload-on-update: true                           # pick up rotated certificates without a restart
server:
  ssl: { bundle: server, client-auth: want }           # mutual TLS when the client presents a certificate
  port: 8443

# cert-manager issues and renews certificates
# apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1  kind: Certificate  spec: { secretName: catalogue-tls, issuerRef: { name: internal-ca }, dnsNames: [ catalogue-service.jsl.svc ] }

# Ingress with Let's Encrypt
# annotations: { cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt }   tls: [ { hosts: [ api.javaschoollab.com ], secretName: api-tls } ]

intermediate.content:
Secrets management

• Secrets (DB passwords, API keys, signing keys, client secrets) must never be in source control, images, logs or plain ConfigMaps. Options: HashiCorp Vault (dynamic short-lived DB credentials, PKI, encryption as a service, audit), cloud secret managers (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager), Kubernetes Secrets (base64 only: enable encryption at rest, RBAC, and sync from a real vault with External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver; use Sealed Secrets for GitOps).
• Practices: least privilege access per service, rotation, short-lived credentials, no shared credentials between services, scan repos for leaked secrets (gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning), mask secrets in logs/actuator (management.endpoint.env.show-values=never), and rotate immediately after exposure.
codeExamples:
# External Secrets Operator: pull from Vault / AWS into a Kubernetes Secret
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata: { name: catalogue-db }
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef: { name: vault-backend, kind: ClusterSecretStore }
  target: { name: catalogue-db-secret }
  data: [ { secretKey: password, remoteRef: { key: secret/catalogue/db, property: password } } ]

# Spring Cloud Vault with dynamic DB credentials (lease-based, auto-rotated)
spring:
  config.import: "vault://"
  cloud.vault:
    uri: https://vault:8200
    authentication: KUBERNETES
    kubernetes: { role: catalogue, service-account-token-file: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token }
    database: { enabled: true, role: catalogue-readwrite, backend: database }

management.endpoint.env.show-values: never          # actuator /env must not reveal secrets

expert.content:
Keycloak integration

• Keycloak is an open-source identity and access management server: realms (isolated user/client spaces), clients (applications: public SPA with PKCE, confidential backend, service account), users/groups/roles (realm roles and client roles), mappers (add claims to tokens), social login, MFA, user federation (LDAP), SSO, admin console/API, token lifetimes, brute-force protection. Run it with PostgreSQL in production (and behind HTTPS).
• Integration: services are resource servers (issuer-uri: https://auth/realms/jsl); the SPA/BFF uses the Authorization Code + PKCE flow (oauth2Login in a Spring Boot BFF, or keycloak-js/angular-oauth2-oidc/oidc-client-ts); service accounts use client credentials. Map Keycloak roles (realm_access.roles, resource_access.<client>.roles) to Spring authorities. Export the realm as JSON for repeatable environments (Keycloak import/Terraform provider).

interviewQA: How do you manage secrets in microservices?

Keep them out of code and images; use a secret manager (Vault, cloud secret stores) or Kubernetes Secrets synced from one (External Secrets/CSI), with least-privilege access, rotation, short-lived credentials and audit, and never expose them via logs or actuator.
What is mTLS and why use it between services?
Mutual TLS makes both sides present certificates, so each service authenticates the other and traffic is encrypted. A service mesh automates certificate issuance and rotation.
What are Keycloak realms and clients?
A realm is an isolated space of users, roles and clients; a client is an application registered in the realm (SPA with PKCE, confidential backend, or service account) that requests tokens.

topics.name: CAP Theorem and Consistency Models

beginner.content:
CAP theorem

• In a distributed data store you can provide at most two of three: Consistency (every read sees the latest write: linearizability), Availability (every request to a non-failing node gets a response) and Partition tolerance (the system continues despite network partitions). Network partitions will happen, so the real choice during a partition is CP (refuse/err to stay consistent) or AP (answer with possibly stale data).
• Examples: CP: ZooKeeper, etcd, Consul KV, HBase, MongoDB (default majority), relational primary with sync replication. AP: Cassandra, DynamoDB (eventual), Eureka, Couchbase. Without a partition you still trade latency vs consistency (PACELC): E: else (no partition) choose Latency or Consistency.
codeExamples:
Consistency
           /\
          /  \          CP: etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul (reject writes without quorum)
         /____\         AP: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Eureka (serve possibly stale data)
 Availability  Partition tolerance (not optional in a distributed system)

 During a partition: pick CP (some requests fail) or AP (all succeed, data may diverge, reconcile later)
 Normal operation (PACELC): lower latency (async replication, stale reads) vs stronger consistency (sync replication, slower)

intermediate.content:
Consistency models

ModelGuaranteeExample / cost
Strong / linearizableOperations appear to happen atomically in real-time order; reads see the latest writeSingle-leader DB with sync reads, Spanner, etcd: higher latency
SequentialAll see operations in one agreed order (not necessarily real time)ZooKeeper
CausalCausally related operations are seen in order by everyoneMongoDB causal sessions, social comments after posts
Read-your-writesA client sees its own updatesRoute reads to the primary after a write
Monotonic readsNo going back in time on repeated readsSticky replica sessions
EventualReplicas converge if updates stopCassandra, DNS, read replicas: highest availability
• Choose per use case: balances/inventory need strong consistency (or compensation); likes counts, feeds and search tolerate eventual. Mixed systems: strong for the write path (single leader), eventual for read replicas/caches/projections.

expert.content:
Designing for eventual consistency

• Techniques: version numbers/vector clocks to detect conflicts, CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types: counters, sets), last-write-wins (with the risk of lost updates), read repair, anti-entropy, quorum reads/writes (R + W > N gives strong consistency in quorum systems), idempotent and commutative operations, compensation for business invariants.
• UX: show pending states, avoid showing contradictory data, give feedback when convergence completes, and place consistency boundaries within a single aggregate/service.
• In Spring: DB isolation + optimistic locking within a service; sagas/outbox across services; cache TTLs and invalidation events for caches; read replicas with awareness of replication lag.

interviewQA: What does the CAP theorem say?

During a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency (stale or failed requests are rejected) and availability (every request answered, possibly with stale data); partition tolerance is unavoidable.
What is eventual consistency?
A model where replicas may differ temporarily but converge to the same value if no new updates arrive; it favours availability and latency.
When is strong consistency required?
For invariants such as account balances, inventory counts and uniqueness constraints, where stale or conflicting data causes incorrect business outcomes; other data can be eventually consistent.

topics.name: Distributed Locking, Idempotent Consumers, Duplicate Messages and Event Ordering

beginner.content:
Distributed locking

• A distributed lock gives mutual exclusion across instances (only one instance runs a job, updates a shared resource). Implementations: database (row lock SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, advisory locks, unique-row "lock table"), Redis (SET key value NX PX ttl; Redisson RLock; Redlock is debated), ZooKeeper/etcd/Consul (ephemeral nodes/leases: stronger), ShedLock for scheduled jobs (DB/Redis-backed).
• Pitfalls: locks must expire (TTL) or a crashed holder blocks everyone; a paused holder (GC, network) can resume after expiry and corrupt data: use fencing tokens (monotonic token checked by the resource); clocks and timeouts; lock granularity; prefer lock-free designs (optimistic concurrency, partitioning work by key so one consumer owns a key, idempotent operations).

intermediate.content:
Idempotent consumers and duplicate message handling

• Brokers are at-least-once: duplicates happen (producer retries, consumer crash after processing before commit, rebalances). A consumer must produce the same outcome when it processes the same message twice.
• Techniques: (1) naturally idempotent writes (upsert, set status to X); (2) inbox table: insert the message id (unique) in the same transaction as the business change; if the insert violates uniqueness, skip; (3) conditional updates with versions (where version = ?); (4) deduplication window in a cache (Redis SETNX with TTL) when strict storage is overkill; (5) idempotency keys in downstream APIs; (6) producer idempotence (enable.idempotence=true) removes producer-side duplicates inside Kafka. Commit offsets after processing.

expert.content:
Event ordering

• Kafka guarantees order within a partition only: use a key (entity id) so all events of an entity land in one partition and are processed in order by one consumer. Across keys/partitions there is no global order. RabbitMQ preserves order per queue but concurrent consumers and redelivery can reorder.
• Handle out-of-order and late events: include a sequence number/version and timestamp in events; ignore stale events (if event.version <= current.version skip); buffer and reorder where necessary; design events so they are commutative or carry full state (event-carried state transfer).
• Retries and ordering: a retry topic can reorder messages (a failed message is retried later while newer ones pass): decide if per-key order matters; for strict ordering block the partition (stop-on-error) with a DLT fallback and alerts.

interviewQA: How do you prevent duplicate message processing?
Make consumers idempotent: record processed message ids in an inbox table within the same transaction, use naturally idempotent upserts or conditional updates, and commit offsets after processing.
Why are distributed locks risky?
Locks can expire while the holder is paused and resume, causing two owners; use TTLs, fencing tokens and prefer lock-free designs (optimistic concurrency, partitioning by key, idempotency).
How do you preserve event order in Kafka?
Use the entity id as the message key so all its events go to the same partition, consumed sequentially by one consumer; add versions to detect stale or out-of-order events.

topics.name: Clock Synchronization, Leader Election and Split-Brain Problems

beginner.content:
Clocks in distributed systems

• Machine clocks drift and differ (NTP keeps them within milliseconds, but can jump). So wall-clock timestamps cannot reliably order events across machines, and "the latest timestamp wins" can silently lose data.
• Tools: logical clocks (Lamport timestamps: a counter that gives a consistent order consistent with causality), vector clocks (detect concurrent/conflicting updates), hybrid logical clocks (HLC: physical time + logical counter, used by CockroachDB), TrueTime (Spanner: bounded clock uncertainty), per-aggregate version numbers, DB sequences, monotonic clocks for measuring durations (System.nanoTime), UTC Instant everywhere and NTP monitoring.
• Rule: use timestamps for display and TTLs, not for ordering or correctness; use versions/sequences for that.

intermediate.content:
Leader election

• Some tasks need exactly one leader: a scheduler, a partition owner, a primary database, a cache refresher. Leader election picks one node and re-elects when it fails. Algorithms: Raft and Paxos (consensus), Zab (ZooKeeper); in practice use a coordination service: ZooKeeper/etcd/Consul (sessions/leases/ephemeral keys), Kubernetes Lease objects, Redis with TTL (weaker), or a database lock row with a lease.
• Requirements: lease with TTL and heartbeats (the leader must keep renewing), fencing tokens so a stale ex-leader cannot act, fast failover vs flapping tradeoff, and idempotent leader actions. Spring: Spring Integration LockRegistryLeaderInitiator, Spring Cloud Kubernetes leader election, Spring Cloud Zookeeper/Consul leader, ShedLock for simple jobs.

expert.content:
Split-brain problems

• Split-brain: after a network partition two groups of nodes each believe they are the leader/primary, accept writes and diverge (double processing, conflicting data, duplicate cron jobs, two primaries in a database cluster).
• Prevention: quorum/majority decisions (a leader needs more than half the votes: with 2 partitions at most one side has a majority: use an odd number of nodes, 3 or 5), fencing (STONITH: shoot the other node; fence tokens at the resource; revoke leases), leases with expiry (a leader stops acting when it cannot renew), witness/arbiter nodes, avoiding two-node clusters, health checks via a majority view, and designing for idempotent/mergeable operations (CRDTs) when AP is chosen.
• Detection and recovery: monitor divergence, run reconciliation/repair jobs, document manual runbooks.
• Related: Eureka's self-preservation and Redis Sentinel/Cluster failover behaviours are split-brain trade-offs: know your tools' guarantees.
codeExamples:
3-node cluster, partition isolates node A from B and C:
   [A]   |   [B] [C]
   A: minority (1 of 3) -> cannot be leader, becomes read-only / stops
   B+C: majority (2 of 3) -> elect a new leader, continue
 => at most ONE side can make progress (no split-brain). With 2 nodes no side has a majority after a partition => do not run 2-node clusters.

# Kafka: min.insync.replicas=2, replication.factor=3, acks=all  -> a partitioned leader without 2 in-sync replicas rejects writes (CP behaviour for durability)
# PostgreSQL HA: Patroni with etcd (consensus) prevents two primaries; use fencing/watchdog on the old primary

interviewQA: Why can't timestamps be used to order events across services?
Clocks drift and can jump, so wall-clock times from different machines are not reliably comparable; use per-aggregate versions, sequences or logical/hybrid clocks for ordering.
What is split-brain and how do you prevent it?

A partition leaves two nodes or groups both acting as leader, accepting conflicting writes. Prevent with quorum/majority elections (odd cluster sizes), leases, fencing tokens and avoiding two-node clusters.
How is leader election typically implemented?
With a consensus-backed coordination service (ZooKeeper, etcd, Consul, Kubernetes Leases) using leases/ephemeral keys and heartbeats, plus fencing tokens so a stale leader cannot act.

topics.name: Centralized Logging, ELK Stack and Correlation IDs

beginner.content:
Centralized logging

• With many instances that appear and disappear, reading log files on servers is impossible. Centralised logging ships all logs to one searchable store. Containers log to stdout/stderr; a node agent (Fluent Bit/Filebeat/Vector/Promtail) collects and forwards to a backend: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (ELK/EFK) or Grafana Loki (cheaper, label-indexed).
• Log as structured JSON with fields: timestamp, level, service, version, environment, traceId/spanId, correlation id, user id (not PII), logger, message, exception. Consistent field names (ECS/OpenTelemetry semantic conventions) make cross-service queries possible. Set retention and sampling; protect PII.
codeExamples:
# Spring Boot 3.4 structured logging
logging.structured.format.console: ecs                  # or logstash / gelf
logging.structured.ecs.service.name: catalogue-service
logging.level.com.javaschoollab: INFO

# example log line (ECS JSON)
# {"@timestamp":"2026-10-20T10:15:30.123Z","log.level":"ERROR","service.name":"catalogue-service","trace.id":"4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
#  "span.id":"00f067aa0ba902b7","message":"Course 42 not found","error.type":"CourseNotFoundException"}

# Logback JSON for older versions: logstash-logback-encoder
# <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder"><customFields>{"service":"catalogue-service"}</customFields></encoder>

intermediate.content:
The ELK stack

• Elasticsearch (store + search), Logstash (pipeline: parse/enrich; often replaced by Beats/Fluent Bit + ingest pipelines), Kibana (search UI, dashboards, alerts); Beats/Elastic Agent collect. EFK = Fluentd/Fluent Bit instead of Logstash. Flow: app (stdout JSON) → Fluent Bit DaemonSet → (Kafka buffer optional) → Elasticsearch → Kibana.
• Operate carefully: index templates and ILM (rollover daily/size, hot-warm-cold, delete after N days), shard sizing, mapping explosions (do not index unbounded field names), a buffer (Kafka) to absorb bursts, security (TLS, authN, RBAC), and cost control (drop DEBUG, sample, shorter retention). Loki indexes only labels (service, level) and stores log lines compressed: great with Grafana and much cheaper.
codeExamples:
# Fluent Bit (Kubernetes DaemonSet) -> Elasticsearch
[INPUT]
    Name tail
    Path /var/log/containers/*.log
    Parser docker
    Tag kube.*
[FILTER]
    Name kubernetes
    Match kube.*
    Merge_Log On              # parse the app's JSON line into fields
[OUTPUT]
    Name es
    Match kube.*
    Host elasticsearch
    Logstash_Format On
    Logstash_Prefix jsl-logs

# Kibana (KQL): follow one request across services
# trace.id: "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736" and log.level: ("ERROR" or "WARN")

# ILM policy: rollover at 30 GB or 1 day, delete after 14 days
# PUT _ilm/policy/jsl-logs {"policy":{"phases":{"hot":{"actions":{"rollover":{"max_size":"30gb","max_age":"1d"}}},"delete":{"min_age":"14d","actions":{"delete":{}}}}}}

expert.content:
Correlation IDs

• A correlation id (request id) is generated at the edge (gateway) for each incoming request (or taken from X-Correlation-Id/traceparent), propagated on every outgoing HTTP call and message header, and added to every log line (MDC). Searching one id shows the whole journey across services: indispensable for troubleshooting. Distributed tracing (traceparent W3C header with trace id/span id) supersedes and automates this; keep a business correlation id (order id) as an extra field.
• Implementation: gateway/servlet filter sets MDC; Micrometer Tracing does it automatically for traces and propagates through RestClient, WebClient, Feign, Kafka and @Async (with context propagation). Return the id in error responses so users/support can quote it; clear MDC after requests (thread reuse).

interviewQA: Why is centralised logging necessary in microservices?
Instances are ephemeral and numerous, so logs must be shipped from stdout to a central searchable store (ELK, Loki) with structured fields and trace ids to troubleshoot across services.
What is a correlation id?

A unique id attached to a request at the edge and propagated through all services and log lines, so you can find every log entry and call belonging to one user request. Distributed tracing formalises this with trace and span ids.
What are the main ELK components?
Elasticsearch stores and searches logs, Logstash (or Beats/Fluent Bit) collects and transforms them, and Kibana visualises, searches and alerts; Loki with Grafana is a lighter alternative.

topics.name: Metrics: Micrometer, Prometheus and Grafana

beginner.content:
Micrometer and Actuator metrics

• Micrometer is the vendor-neutral metrics facade (like SLF4J for metrics) built into Spring Boot Actuator. It exposes JVM, HTTP server/client, datasource pool (Hikari), Kafka, cache, Resilience4j and custom metrics, and exports to Prometheus, Datadog, New Relic, CloudWatch, etc. Add micrometer-registry-prometheus and expose /actuator/prometheus.
• Meter types: Counter (only goes up: requests, errors), Gauge (current value: queue size, active sessions), Timer (duration + count + percentiles: latency), DistributionSummary (sizes), LongTaskTimer. Use tags (dimensions) with bounded cardinality: never put user ids or raw URLs in tags (cardinality explosion).

intermediate.content:
Prometheus

• Prometheus is a time-series database that scrapes (pulls) /metrics endpoints at an interval, stores samples with labels, and answers PromQL queries; Alertmanager routes alerts (Slack, PagerDuty, e-mail). On Kubernetes use the Prometheus Operator (kube-prometheus-stack) with ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor objects for discovery.
• PromQL essentials: rate(counter[5m]) (per-second rate), histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(..._bucket[5m]))) (p95 latency), sum by (service) (...), ratios for error rate. Monitor the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation (and RED for services: Rate, Errors, Duration; USE for resources: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors).
codeExamples:
# ServiceMonitor: Prometheus scrapes every pod of the service
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata: { name: catalogue }
spec:
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: catalogue } }
  endpoints: [ { port: http, path: /actuator/prometheus, interval: 15s } ]

# PromQL
# Request rate per service:       sum by (application) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m]))
# Error ratio (5xx):               sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m]))
# p95 latency:                     histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket{application="catalogue-service"}[5m])))
# Hikari saturation:               hikaricp_connections_active / hikaricp_connections_max
# JVM heap used %:                 jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"} / jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="heap"}

expert.content:
Grafana dashboards and alerting

• Grafana visualises Prometheus (and Loki, Tempo, Elasticsearch, etc.): dashboards per service (RED + JVM + DB pool + Kafka lag + circuit breakers), a service overview, and an SLO dashboard. Provision dashboards as code (JSON/Grafonnet in Git). Use the community JVM (Micrometer) and Spring Boot dashboards as a start.
• Alerting: alert on symptoms users feel (error ratio, latency SLO burn, availability), not on every cause (CPU at 80%); give each alert an owner, severity, runbook link and a for: duration to avoid flapping; page only for urgent, actionable issues; route the rest to tickets/Slack. SLOs/error budgets: define targets (99.9% of requests under 500 ms), alert on burn rate (multi-window).
• Avoid alert fatigue: review noisy alerts, deduplicate in Alertmanager (grouping, inhibition, silences).
codeExamples:
# Prometheus alert rules
groups:
- name: catalogue
  rules:
  - alert: HighErrorRate
    expr: sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="catalogue-service",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="catalogue-service"}[5m])) > 0.05
    for: 5m
    labels: { severity: page }
    annotations: { summary: "catalogue-service 5xx > 5% for 5m", runbook: "https://wiki/runbooks/catalogue-5xx" }
  - alert: SlowP95
    expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket{application="catalogue-service"}[5m]))) > 1
    for: 10m
    labels: { severity: warn }
  - alert: ConsumerLagGrowing
    expr: sum(kafka_consumergroup_lag{group="learning"}) > 10000
    for: 10m
    labels: { severity: warn }
  - alert: PodCrashLooping
    expr: increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{namespace="jsl"}[15m]) > 3

interviewQA: What are the four golden signals?
Latency, traffic, errors and saturation: the key indicators of a service's health. RED (rate, errors, duration) is the service-focused subset.
What does Micrometer do?
It is a vendor-neutral metrics facade in Spring Boot that records counters, gauges, timers and summaries and exports them to Prometheus, Datadog and other systems.
What should you alert on?
User-visible symptoms such as error rate, latency and availability against SLOs, each with an owner and runbook, rather than every internal cause like moderate CPU usage, to avoid alert fatigue.

topics.name: Distributed Tracing: OpenTelemetry, Zipkin, Jaeger and Micrometer Tracing

beginner.content:
Distributed tracing concepts

• A trace follows one request across services; it is made of spans: a span = one operation (an HTTP handler, a DB query, a Kafka publish/consume) with start/end time, attributes (tags), events and a parent span id. All spans of a request share a trace id. Context is propagated in headers: W3C Trace Context traceparent: 00-<traceId>-<spanId>-01 (B3 for Zipkin legacy).
• Tracing answers: where was the time spent?, which downstream call failed?, what is the dependency graph?. Metrics tell you that something is slow; traces show where; logs show why (correlated by trace id).
• Sampling: tracing every request is expensive. Head sampling (decide at the start: e.g. 10%) is cheap; tail sampling (decide after seeing the whole trace: keep errors and slow ones) in the OpenTelemetry Collector is smarter.
codeExamples:
trace 4bf92f35...  total 480 ms
 |- gateway               GET /api/learning/progress               [0 ms ....................... 480 ms]
 |   '- learning-service   GET /progress                           [12 ms ................... 470 ms]
 |       |- postgres        SELECT progress ...                    [20 ms .. 60 ms]
 |       '- catalogue-service  GET /courses?ids=...                 [70 ms ............. 440 ms]   <- slow
 |           '- postgres    SELECT course ...                      [80 ms ....... 420 ms]            <- the real culprit: slow query

intermediate.content:
OpenTelemetry and Micrometer Tracing in Spring Boot 3

• OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the CNCF standard for traces, metrics and logs: APIs/SDKs, the OTLP protocol, auto-instrumentation agent (Java agent: -javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar instruments HTTP, JDBC, Kafka... with no code changes) and the OpenTelemetry Collector (receive, process, sample, export to Jaeger/Tempo/Zipkin/Datadog).
• Spring Boot 3 uses Micrometer Tracing (replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth) with a bridge to OpenTelemetry: add micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel + opentelemetry-exporter-otlp (or spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry in newer versions), enable observation of HTTP, RestClient, WebClient, Feign, Kafka (spring.kafka.template.observation-enabled=true) and JDBC (datasource-micrometer). Set sampling and the OTLP endpoint.
codeExamples:
<dependency><groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId><artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>io.micrometer</groupId><artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel</artifactId></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>io.opentelemetry</groupId><artifactId>opentelemetry-exporter-otlp</artifactId></dependency>

management:
  tracing:
    sampling.probability: 0.1                      # 10% head sampling (use 1.0 in dev)
  otlp.tracing.endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
spring:
  application.name: catalogue-service
  kafka.template.observation-enabled: true         # propagate trace context through Kafka headers
  kafka.listener.observation-enabled: true
logging.pattern.level: "%5p [${spring.application.name:},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}]"

// custom span for a business operation
@Service
class CertificateService {
    private final ObservationRegistry registry;
    byte[] generate(UUID id) {
        return Observation.createNotStarted("certificate.generate", registry).lowCardinalityKeyValue("type", "pdf").observe(() -> render(id));
    }
}

expert.content:
Zipkin, Jaeger and the Collector pipeline

• Zipkin and Jaeger are tracing backends with UIs: search by trace id/service/duration/tag, view waterfall timelines and the service dependency graph; Jaeger (CNCF) supports OTLP natively, adaptive sampling, and Elasticsearch/Cassandra/OpenSearch storage; Zipkin is simple and light. Grafana Tempo stores traces cheaply (object storage) and links to logs (Loki) and metrics (exemplars).
• Typical pipeline: services → OTLP → OpenTelemetry Collector (batch, tail-sample, enrich with k8s metadata) → Jaeger/Tempo; logs carry traceId so Grafana can jump from a log line to the trace.
• Practices: propagate context through async boundaries (messaging headers, @Async with ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator, virtual threads), put the trace id in error responses and logs, keep attribute cardinality low, never put PII in spans.

interviewQA: How do you trace requests across microservices?

Instrument services with OpenTelemetry/Micrometer Tracing so each hop creates spans sharing a trace id propagated via W3C traceparent headers (including messaging headers), export to a backend such as Jaeger/Tempo/Zipkin and correlate logs with the trace id.
What are traces and spans?
A trace represents one request end to end; it is composed of spans, each a timed operation with attributes and a parent span, forming a tree across services.
What is tail sampling?

Deciding which traces to keep after they complete (for example errors and slow requests) in the OpenTelemetry Collector, unlike head sampling which decides at the start and may drop the interesting traces.

topics.name: Health Checks, Spring Boot Actuator and Alerting & Dashboards

beginner.content:
Spring Boot Actuator

• Actuator adds production-ready endpoints: /actuator/health (liveness/readiness, details), info, metrics, prometheus, loggers (change log levels at runtime), env/configprops (mask secrets), threaddump, heapdump, httpexchanges, scheduledtasks, caches, flyway, circuitbreakers. Only health, info and prometheus should be exposed over the network; secure everything else (separate management port, authentication, network policy).
• Health groups for Kubernetes: management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true gives /actuator/health/liveness (is the process alive? restart if not) and /readiness (can it take traffic? remove from the Service if not). Include only what each probe should depend on.
codeExamples:
management:
  server.port: 9090                                      # separate management port, not exposed by the Ingress
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,prometheus,loggers
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes.enabled: true
      show-details: when-authorized
      group:
        liveness:  { include: livenessState }                         # JVM/app state only: do NOT include the database
        readiness: { include: readinessState,db,diskSpace }           # ready only when the database is reachable
    env.show-values: never
  info.env.enabled: true
info.app: { name: catalogue-service, version: "@project.version@" }

@Component
class KafkaHealth implements HealthIndicator {
    public Health health() { return broker.isReachable() ? Health.up().withDetail("brokers", 3).build() : Health.down().withDetail("reason", "no broker").build(); }
}

# change a log level at runtime without a restart
# curl -X POST localhost:9090/actuator/loggers/com.javaschoollab -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'

intermediate.content:
Health check design

• Liveness vs readiness vs startup: liveness = "is it stuck? restart me" (must not depend on external services: a database outage must not restart every pod); readiness = "send me traffic?" (can include required dependencies; fail temporarily during startup, warm-up, overload or shutdown); startup probe for slow starts.
• Deep health checks (calling the database on every probe) can amplify outages; use short timeouts, caching of results (management.endpoint.health.cache.time-to-live) and a separate diagnostic endpoint for humans. Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM readiness turns DOWN first, in-flight requests finish, then exit.
• External monitoring: synthetic checks (probe the public URL/login flow from outside), uptime services, and heartbeat jobs.
codeExamples:
# Kubernetes probes using Actuator
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9090 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 20
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 9090 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9090 }
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 5                                        # up to 150 s to start before liveness takes over
lifecycle:
  preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 10"] } }  # let the load balancer drain
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45

# application.yml
server.shutdown: graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s

expert.content:
Alerting and dashboards in practice

• Build a layered set of dashboards: (1) business/SLO (enrolments per minute, checkout success rate), (2) service RED (rate, errors, duration), (3) dependencies (DB pool, Kafka lag, circuit breakers, external APIs), (4) infrastructure (CPU, memory, pods, nodes). Link dashboards to logs and traces (Grafana data links, exemplars).
• Alert routing: Alertmanager groups alerts, silences during maintenance, escalates by severity to PagerDuty/Opsgenie/Slack; every page needs a runbook and an owner; after incidents write post-mortems and fix the alert or the system.
• Alert on SLO burn rate (fast: 14.4× over 1 h; slow: 6× over 6 h) to be both quick and quiet; include deadman/heartbeat alerts (alert when metrics stop arriving) and synthetic probes so a dead monitoring pipeline is noticed.
codeExamples:
# Alertmanager routing
route:
  receiver: slack-default
  group_by: [alertname, application]
  group_wait: 30s
  repeat_interval: 4h
  routes:
    - matchers: [ severity = page ]
      receiver: pagerduty
    - matchers: [ severity = warn ]
      receiver: slack-default
inhibit_rules:
