  - source_matchers: [ alertname = NodeDown ]
    target_matchers: [ severity = warn ]                    # do not flood with downstream alerts when the node is down
    equal: [ node ]

# SLO burn-rate alert (availability SLO 99.9%)
# expr: (sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[1h])) / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[1h]))) > (14.4 * 0.001)

interviewQA: Liveness vs readiness probe?

Liveness tells Kubernetes whether to restart a stuck container (should not depend on external systems); readiness tells whether it can receive traffic (may depend on required dependencies and is used to add/remove it from the Service).
Which Actuator endpoints should be exposed and how do you secure them?
Expose only health, info and prometheus (ideally on a separate management port or network), require authentication for the rest, hide secret values and never expose heapdump/env publicly.
What makes a good alert?

It signals a user-visible symptom or an imminent SLO breach, is actionable, has an owner, severity, runbook and a duration to avoid flapping, and is routed appropriately; noisy or non-actionable alerts should be removed.

topics.name: Docker Fundamentals, Dockerfile, Docker Compose, Container Networking and Images

beginner.content:
Docker fundamentals

• A container packages an app with its dependencies and runs it isolated using Linux namespaces (process, network, filesystem views) and cgroups (CPU/memory limits), sharing the host kernel: lighter and faster than VMs. An image is a read-only layered template; a container is a running instance; a registry (Docker Hub, ECR, GHCR, Harbor, Artifactory) stores images.
• Why for microservices: identical environments from laptop to production (dev/prod parity), fast start, immutable artifacts, per-service dependencies, simple scaling, the unit Kubernetes schedules.
• Commands: docker build -t catalogue:1.0 ., docker run -p 8081:8081 -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev catalogue:1.0, docker ps, logs -f, exec -it ... sh, stop/rm, images, push.
codeExamples:
docker build -t javaschoollab/catalogue-service:1.0.0 .
docker run -d --name catalogue -p 8081:8081 \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev -e DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://host.docker.internal:5432/catalogue \
  --memory=512m --cpus=1 javaschoollab/catalogue-service:1.0.0
docker logs -f catalogue
docker exec -it catalogue sh
docker stop catalogue && docker rm catalogue
docker push javaschoollab/catalogue-service:1.0.0

intermediate.content:
Writing a good Dockerfile for Spring Boot

• Use a multi-stage build (build with JDK + Maven, run with a small JRE image), a non-root user, layered jar (Spring Boot layertools: dependencies change rarely so they cache well), pinned base image versions (distroless/Temurin/Alpine/Chainguard), correct JVM memory flags for containers (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75), .dockerignore, one process per container, health check, and no secrets in layers.
• Alternatives to a hand-written Dockerfile: Spring Boot Buildpacks (mvn spring-boot:build-image), Jib (builds optimised images without Docker), GraalVM native image (fast start, small memory), CRaC.
codeExamples:
# Dockerfile (multi-stage, layered, non-root)
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY pom.xml mvnw ./
COPY .mvn .mvn
RUN ./mvnw -q dependency:go-offline                  # cached layer until pom.xml changes
COPY src src
RUN ./mvnw -q package -DskipTests && java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/*.jar extract --layers --destination extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd --system --uid 1001 app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /workspace/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /workspace/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build /workspace/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /workspace/extracted/application/ ./
USER app
EXPOSE 8081
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8081/actuator/health/liveness || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "catalogue-service.jar"]

# .dockerignore: target/  .git/  *.md  .idea/

# without a Dockerfile
# ./mvnw spring-boot:build-image -Dspring-boot.build-image.imageName=javaschoollab/catalogue:1.0.0

expert.content:
Docker Compose, networking and image management

• Docker Compose defines a multi-container application in compose.yaml: services, networks, volumes, env, ports, depends_on with healthchecks. Ideal for local development of a microservices system (PostgreSQL, Kafka, Keycloak, services) and integration environments: docker compose up -d.
• Container networking: bridge network (default): containers on a user-defined bridge reach each other by service name via Docker DNS (http://catalogue:8081), expose to the host with ports: "8081:8081"; host (shares the host network), overlay (multi-host, Swarm), none. Inside a container localhost is the container itself: use the service name or host.docker.internal for the host.
• Images: small and secure (JRE not JDK, distroless, no shell tools in prod), tags (immutable version tags + digest; avoid latest in deployments), vulnerability scanning (Trivy), SBOM, signing (cosign), layer caching, registry cleanup policies. Volumes persist data; containers are ephemeral.
codeExamples:
# compose.yaml : local microservices environment
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment: { POSTGRES_USER: jsl, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret, POSTGRES_DB: catalogue }
    volumes: [ pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data ]
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U jsl"], interval: 5s, retries: 10 }
  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:3.8.0
    ports: [ "9092:9092" ]
  catalogue:
    build: ./catalogue-service
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: dev
      DB_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/catalogue          # service name = hostname on the compose network
      KAFKA_BROKERS: kafka:9092
    ports: [ "8081:8081" ]
    depends_on: { postgres: { condition: service_healthy }, kafka: { condition: service_started } }
  gateway:
    build: ./api-gateway
    ports: [ "8080:8080" ]
    depends_on: [ catalogue ]
volumes: { pgdata: {} }

# docker compose up -d --build     docker compose logs -f catalogue     docker compose down -v

interviewQA: Docker image vs container?
An image is a read-only layered template containing the app and its dependencies; a container is a running instance of an image with its own writable layer, process and network namespace.
What are the best practices for a Spring Boot Dockerfile?
Multi-stage build, small JRE base image with a pinned version, non-root user, layered jar for caching, container-aware JVM flags, .dockerignore, health check, and no secrets in the image.
How do containers on one Docker network reach each other?
By service/container name through Docker's embedded DNS on a user-defined bridge network; localhost inside a container refers to the container itself.

topics.name: Kubernetes Fundamentals: Pods, Deployments, Services and Ingress

beginner.content:
Kubernetes architecture and core objects

• Kubernetes orchestrates containers across a cluster: scheduling, scaling, self-healing, rollouts, service discovery, config and storage. Control plane: API server, etcd (state), scheduler, controller manager; nodes run the kubelet, container runtime and kube-proxy.
• Declarative model: you describe the desired state in YAML (kubectl apply -f); controllers continuously reconcile actual state to it.
• Core objects: Pod (one or more containers sharing network/storage; the smallest unit; ephemeral), ReplicaSet (keeps N pods), Deployment (manages ReplicaSets: rollouts, rollbacks), Service (stable virtual IP/DNS + load balancing to pods by label), Ingress (HTTP routing from outside), Namespace, ConfigMap/Secret, Job/CronJob, StatefulSet (stable identity/storage for databases), DaemonSet.
codeExamples:
kubectl get pods,svc,deploy -n jsl
kubectl apply -f k8s/                          # declarative: create/update from files
kubectl describe pod catalogue-6d5f7c9b8-xk2lp # events, probes, why it is Pending/CrashLooping
kubectl logs -f deploy/catalogue --tail=100
kubectl exec -it deploy/catalogue -- sh
kubectl port-forward svc/catalogue 8081:80     # reach a service from your laptop
kubectl rollout status deploy/catalogue && kubectl rollout undo deploy/catalogue
kubectl top pods                                # needs metrics-server

intermediate.content:
Pods and Deployments

• A Deployment declares a pod template, replicas, a label selector and the update strategy (RollingUpdate: maxSurge, maxUnavailable). Always set resource requests and limits (requests drive scheduling; limits cap usage: a container over its memory limit is OOMKilled), probes, a security context (non-root, read-only filesystem) and labels. Never run bare Pods in production.
• Use immutable image tags (version or digest); spread replicas across nodes/zones (topologySpreadConstraints, anti-affinity); a PodDisruptionBudget keeps a minimum available during node drains.

expert.content:
Services and Ingress

• A Service gives pods a stable name and load-balances to ready pods matching its selector. Types: ClusterIP (internal; default), NodePort (port on every node), LoadBalancer (cloud LB), ExternalName; headless (clusterIP: None) returns pod IPs (StatefulSets, client-side balancing). Inside the cluster services are reachable as http://catalogue (same namespace) or catalogue.jsl.svc.cluster.local: this is your service discovery.
• Ingress (or the newer Gateway API) routes external HTTP(S) traffic to Services by host/path through an ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, Envoy/Contour, cloud ALB), terminates TLS (cert-manager) and applies annotations (rate limits, timeouts). Often the Ingress points to your Spring Cloud Gateway (single entry) or routes directly to services.
codeExamples:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: catalogue, namespace: jsl }
spec:
  selector: { app: catalogue }
  ports: [ { name: http, port: 80, targetPort: http } ]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: jsl
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "30"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls: [ { hosts: [ api.javaschoollab.com ], secretName: api-tls } ]
  rules:
    - host: api.javaschoollab.com
      http:
        paths:
          - { path: /api/courses, pathType: Prefix, backend: { service: { name: catalogue, port: { number: 80 } } } }
          - { path: /api/learning, pathType: Prefix, backend: { service: { name: learning, port: { number: 80 } } } }

interviewQA: Pod vs Deployment vs Service?

A Pod is the smallest runnable unit (one or more containers); a Deployment manages replicated Pods with rolling updates and rollbacks; a Service gives a set of Pods a stable name/IP and load-balances traffic to the ready ones.
What is the difference between Service and Ingress?
A Service exposes pods inside the cluster (or via NodePort/LoadBalancer) at L4; an Ingress routes external HTTP(S) traffic by host and path to Services through an ingress controller and handles TLS.
Why set resource requests and limits?
Requests let the scheduler place pods and guarantee capacity; limits cap usage (exceeding memory kills the container). Without them pods can starve or be evicted unpredictably.

topics.name: ConfigMaps and Secrets, Horizontal Pod Autoscaling, Probes and Rolling Deployments

beginner.content:
ConfigMaps and Secrets

• ConfigMap: non-sensitive configuration (key/values or files) injected as environment variables (envFrom), files in a mounted volume, or command args. Secret: sensitive data (passwords, tokens, TLS keys): base64-encoded (not encrypted by default): enable encryption at rest, restrict RBAC, prefer external managers (Vault, External Secrets, Sealed Secrets). Mounted files update when the object changes (env vars do not): pods usually need a rolling restart (kubectl rollout restart, Reloader, or Spring Cloud Kubernetes reload).
• Spring mapping: env SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL ↔ spring.datasource.url; mounted application.yml via spring.config.import=optional:file:/config/.
codeExamples:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: catalogue-config, namespace: jsl }
data:
  SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod
  JSL_CATALOGUE_MAX_PAGE_SIZE: "100"
  application.yml: |
    jsl.pricing.default-currency: INR
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: { name: catalogue-secrets, namespace: jsl }
type: Opaque
stringData:                                   # applied as base64; keep real values out of Git (Sealed/External Secrets)
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: change-me

# in the Deployment
#   envFrom: [ { configMapRef: { name: catalogue-config } }, { secretRef: { name: catalogue-secrets } } ]
#   volumeMounts: [ { name: cfg, mountPath: /config } ]     volumes: [ { name: cfg, configMap: { name: catalogue-config } } ]

intermediate.content:
Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA)

• The HPA adjusts replicas of a Deployment based on metrics: CPU/memory utilisation (needs metrics-server and resource requests), custom metrics (requests per second, queue length/consumer lag via the Prometheus adapter) or external metrics (KEDA scales on Kafka lag, RabbitMQ queue depth, cron, to and from zero). It computes desired = ceil(current × currentMetric / targetMetric) within min/max and with stabilisation windows to prevent flapping.
• Related: VPA (vertical, right-sizes requests), Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter (adds nodes when pods are unschedulable). Design for scaling: stateless pods, fast startup (readiness), graceful shutdown, connection pools sized for N replicas (replicas × pool size ≤ DB max connections).
codeExamples:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: catalogue, namespace: jsl }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: catalogue }
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 12
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 65 } }
    - type: Pods
      pods: { metric: { name: http_server_requests_per_second }, target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "150" } }
  behavior:
    scaleUp:   { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30, policies: [ { type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 30 } ] }
    scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300 }                  # scale down slowly

# KEDA: scale a Kafka consumer on lag (also to zero)
# triggers: [ { type: kafka, metadata: { bootstrapServers: kafka:9092, consumerGroup: learning, topic: payments.events, lagThreshold: "500" } } ]

expert.content:
Readiness and liveness probes, and rolling deployments

• Readiness controls traffic (pod removed from Service endpoints when failing); liveness restarts a stuck container; startup gives slow apps time before liveness applies. Spring Boot Actuator provides /actuator/health/readiness and /liveness (see Observability). A wrong liveness probe (depending on the database) turns a database blip into a restart storm.
• Rolling update: new pods are created and must become ready before old ones are terminated (maxSurge/maxUnavailable); traffic shifts gradually; kubectl rollout undo reverts. Make it zero-downtime: readiness probes, graceful shutdown (server.shutdown=graceful), preStop sleep for endpoint propagation, terminationGracePeriodSeconds > shutdown timeout, backward-compatible DB and API changes (old and new run together), PDBs. Failed rollouts stall (new pods never ready) leaving the old version serving: set progressDeadlineSeconds and alert on it.
codeExamples:
spec:
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300                         # mark the rollout failed if pods are not ready in 5 minutes
  strategy: { type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0 } }
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
      containers:
        - name: catalogue
          lifecycle: { preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 10"] } } }   # keep serving while endpoints are removed everywhere
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8081 }, periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3 }

kubectl set image deploy/catalogue catalogue=ghcr.io/javaschoollab/catalogue-service:1.4.3
kubectl rollout status deploy/catalogue --timeout=5m || kubectl rollout undo deploy/catalogue
kubectl rollout history deploy/catalogue

interviewQA: What do readiness and liveness probes do?
Readiness decides whether a pod receives traffic; liveness decides whether the container should be restarted. Mixing them up (liveness depending on a database) can cause restart storms.
How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler work?
It periodically compares a metric (CPU, custom, external) with a target and scales the Deployment replicas up or down within min/max limits, using stabilisation windows to avoid flapping.
How do you achieve zero-downtime rolling deployments?
Use readiness probes, maxUnavailable 0, graceful shutdown with a preStop delay, PodDisruptionBudgets and backward-compatible database/API changes so old and new versions run side by side.

topics.name: Git and Branching Strategies, Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Build Pipelines and Artifact Repositories

beginner.content:
Git and branching strategies

• Trunk-based development: short-lived branches (hours to 2 days) merged to main via pull requests, feature flags for unfinished work; fits continuous delivery. GitHub Flow: feature branch → PR → review → merge → deploy. Git Flow (develop/release/hotfix) suits scheduled releases but slows CI/CD.
• Repository layout: polyrepo (one repo per service: independent pipelines, clear ownership) vs monorepo (shared code, atomic refactors; needs path-filtered pipelines and tooling like Nx/Bazel/Maven reactor). Protect main: required reviews and status checks, signed commits, no force-push, CODEOWNERS. Conventional Commits + semantic versioning automate changelogs and versions.
codeExamples:
git switch -c feature/enrollment-events
git commit -m "feat(learning): publish EnrollmentCreated via outbox"
git push -u origin feature/enrollment-events          # open a pull request: CI runs, reviewers approve, squash-merge
git tag -a v1.4.2 -m "Release 1.4.2" && git push origin v1.4.2

# CODEOWNERS (required reviewers per service)
# /catalogue-service/   @javaschoollab/catalogue-team
# /payment-service/     @javaschoollab/payments-team @javaschoollab/security

# Branch protection (GitHub): require PR + 1 approval + status checks "build", "test", "sonar"; require linear history

intermediate.content:
Build pipelines: GitHub Actions and Jenkins

• A pipeline per service: checkout → build/compile → unit tests → static analysis (Sonar) → package → build image → scan image → push to registry → deploy to dev → integration/contract tests → deploy to staging → (approval) → production. CI = integrate and verify every change; CD = deliver (always releasable) or deploy (automatically to production).
• GitHub Actions: YAML workflows in .github/workflows, hosted/self-hosted runners, reusable workflows, environments with approvals, OIDC to the cloud (no long-lived keys), caching (actions/setup-java with Maven cache). Jenkins: Jenkinsfile (declarative pipeline), agents (Kubernetes pod agents), shared libraries, a huge plugin ecosystem: common in enterprises. Either way: pipeline as code, ephemeral build agents, fast feedback (< 10 min), no secrets in logs.

expert.content:
Jenkins pipeline and artifact repositories

• Jenkins declarative pipeline: stages with agent (a Kubernetes pod with Maven, Docker/Kaniko), tools, environment using credentials binding, post actions (notify), when conditions (branch), parallel stages, input approval before production, shared libraries for common steps.
• Artifact repositories store build outputs: Maven artifacts (JARs/libraries: Nexus, JFrog Artifactory, GitHub Packages, Maven Central proxy), container images (registry: Harbor, ECR, GHCR, Artifactory), Helm charts (OCI). Benefits: immutable versioned artifacts, caching/proxying upstream, access control, retention and vulnerability metadata, build once, promote the same artifact through environments (never rebuild per environment). Use semantic versions for releases and unique tags (commit SHA) for images; sign and keep an SBOM.

interviewQA: Trunk-based development vs Git Flow?

Trunk-based uses short-lived branches merged to main frequently with feature flags, enabling continuous delivery; Git Flow uses long-lived develop/release branches suited to scheduled releases but slows integration.
What does "build once, deploy many" mean?
Build and test an artifact (image) once, store it immutably in a registry, and promote that same artifact through environments with only configuration changing, instead of rebuilding per environment.
Jenkins vs GitHub Actions?

Both implement pipeline-as-code. GitHub Actions is hosted and tightly integrated with GitHub; Jenkins is a self-hosted, plugin-rich server common in enterprises. Choose by existing tooling, control and compliance needs.

topics.name: Automated Testing in Pipelines, SonarQube, Checkmarx and Container Image Scanning

beginner.content:
Automated testing in the pipeline

• Run the test pyramid automatically: unit (seconds, every commit), integration with Testcontainers (minutes), contract tests (provider verification, consumer stubs), end-to-end/smoke on a deployed environment (few), performance (nightly or pre-release), security (SAST, SCA, DAST). Fail fast: cheap checks first; parallelise; quarantine flaky tests (and fix them); publish reports (JUnit XML, coverage).
• Quality gates: tests pass, coverage on new code (e.g. ≥ 80%), no new blocker/critical issues, no high vulnerabilities, license policy, build reproducible. Mutation testing (PIT) measures test strength.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml: JaCoCo coverage + failsafe for integration tests -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId><artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution><goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution><id>report</id><phase>verify</phase><goals><goal>report</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution><id>check</id><phase>verify</phase><goals><goal>check</goal></goals>
      <configuration><rules><rule><element>BUNDLE</element><limits><limit><counter>LINE</counter><value>COVEREDRATIO</value><minimum>0.75</minimum></limit></limits></rule></rules></configuration></execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
# unit tests: *Test (surefire), integration tests: *IT (failsafe, needs Docker for Testcontainers)
./mvnw -B verify

intermediate.content:
SonarQube and Checkmarx

• SonarQube (static analysis): finds bugs, code smells, security hotspots/vulnerabilities (OWASP rules), duplication and tracks coverage and technical debt. The Quality Gate (conditions on new code) blocks the merge/deploy. Run sonar:sonar in CI with the JaCoCo report; PR decoration comments on diffs. Tune rules and avoid false-positive fatigue; treat the gate as policy.
• Checkmarx (commercial SAST, also SCA/IaC/API security in Checkmarx One): scans source for security flaws (SQL injection, XSS, insecure deserialisation, hard-coded secrets) by analysing data flow; integrates with Jenkins/GitHub, gates on severity, provides remediation guidance. Alternatives: Semgrep, CodeQL (GitHub), Snyk Code, Fortify. SAST (static code) + SCA (dependencies: OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk, Dependabot, Trivy) + DAST (running app: OWASP ZAP) + secret scanning (gitleaks) = layered "shift-left" security.
codeExamples:
# Sonar in the pipeline
./mvnw -B verify sonar:sonar \
  -Dsonar.host.url=https://sonar.jsl.com -Dsonar.token=$SONAR_TOKEN \
  -Dsonar.projectKey=catalogue-service -Dsonar.coverage.jacoco.xmlReportPaths=target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml \
  -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true                       # fail the build if the quality gate fails

# GitHub CodeQL (SAST) + Dependabot (SCA) + gitleaks (secrets)
# - uses: github/codeql-action/init@v3   with: { languages: java }
# - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3
# - uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2

# Checkmarx (CLI) in Jenkins
# sh 'cx scan create --project-name catalogue-service -s . --branch $BRANCH_NAME --threshold "sast-high=1;sast-critical=1"'    # fail on high/critical findings

expert.content:
Container image scanning and supply-chain security

• Scan images for known CVEs in the OS packages and libraries: Trivy (open source, also IaC/secret scan), Grype, Snyk Container, Clair, registry scanners (Harbor/ECR/Artifactory Xray). Scan at build time (fail on HIGH/CRITICAL with a fix available), in the registry continuously (new CVEs appear daily) and at admission time (Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper reject unsigned/vulnerable/latest images).
• Reduce risk: minimal/distroless base images, non-root, no package managers in runtime, pinned versions + digests, regular rebuilds (renovate), SBOM (CycloneDX/SPDX via Syft), image signing (cosign/Sigstore) and provenance (SLSA), private registries, scan IaC (Checkov, tfsec) and Helm charts.
codeExamples:
# Trivy in CI: fail on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed ghcr.io/javaschoollab/catalogue-service:$GITHUB_SHA
trivy fs --scanners vuln,secret,config .                                # repo files, secrets, IaC misconfigurations

# SBOM and signing
syft ghcr.io/javaschoollab/catalogue-service:$GITHUB_SHA -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/javaschoollab/catalogue-service@$DIGEST

# Kubernetes admission policy (Kyverno): only signed images from our registry
# apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1  kind: ClusterPolicy  spec: { validationFailureAction: Enforce, rules: [ { name: verify-signature, match: {...}, verifyImages: [ { imageReferences: ["ghcr.io/javaschoollab/*"], attestors: [ ... ] } ] } ] }

interviewQA: What does SonarQube do and what is a quality gate?

SonarQube statically analyses code for bugs, vulnerabilities, smells, duplication and coverage; a quality gate is a set of pass/fail conditions (usually on new code) that blocks merging or deployment when not met.
SAST vs SCA vs DAST?

SAST analyses your source for security flaws; SCA checks third-party dependencies for known vulnerabilities and licenses; DAST tests the running application from outside. Together they provide layered shift-left security.
How do you secure container images?
Use minimal pinned base images, run as non-root, scan for CVEs in build and registry, generate SBOMs, sign images and enforce admission policies so only trusted, scanned images run.

topics.name: Blue-Green, Canary Deployments and Rollback Strategies

beginner.content:
Deployment strategies compared

StrategyHowProsCons
RollingReplace instances graduallyNo extra capacity, default in KubernetesTwo versions live together; slower rollback
Blue-GreenTwo full environments; switch traffic from blue (old) to green (new)Instant switch and rollback, test green before exposing2× infrastructure, database compatibility, session/cache warm-up
CanarySend a small % of traffic to the new version, increase while metrics are healthyReal-traffic validation, limited blast radiusNeeds traffic splitting + metrics/automation
RecreateStop old, start newSimpleDowntime
Shadow / dark launchMirror traffic to the new version without returning its responsesSafe performance/behaviour testSide effects must be disabled
Feature flagsDeploy code off; enable per user/percentageDecouples deploy from releaseFlag debt, testing combinations

intermediate.content:
Blue-green and canary on Kubernetes

• Blue-green: run two Deployments (catalogue-blue, catalogue-green) and point the Service/Ingress selector to one; switch by changing the selector label or Ingress backend; keep blue for fast rollback. Canary: Argo Rollouts or Flagger automate traffic shifting (5% → 25% → 50% → 100%) with an analysis step querying Prometheus (error rate, latency) and auto-rollback on failure; ingress-nginx canary annotations or a mesh (Istio VirtualService weights) split traffic.
• Database changes must be backward compatible (expand/contract) because old and new versions run at the same time.
codeExamples:
# Argo Rollouts: canary with automated analysis
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata: { name: catalogue }
spec:
  replicas: 5
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: catalogue } }
  template: { metadata: { labels: { app: catalogue } }, spec: { containers: [ { name: catalogue, image: ghcr.io/javaschoollab/catalogue-service:1.5.0 } ] } }
  strategy:
    canary:
      canaryService: catalogue-canary
      stableService: catalogue-stable
      trafficRouting: { istio: { virtualService: { name: catalogue-vs } } }
      steps:
        - setWeight: 5
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - analysis: { templates: [ { templateName: success-rate } ] }     # Prometheus query: error rate < 1%
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }                                          # then 100%; any failed analysis => automatic rollback

# Blue-green switch with a Service selector
# kubectl patch svc catalogue -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"catalogue","version":"green"}}}'

expert.content:
Rollback strategies

• Always plan the way back before deploying. Fast rollback options: kubectl rollout undo / Helm rollback / Argo CD revert to the previous Git commit (GitOps), switch blue-green back, set canary weight to 0, disable a feature flag (fastest, no deploy). Automate: health-gated rollouts (stop and revert when readiness/error-rate thresholds are breached), progressive delivery, synthetic checks after deploy.
• Hard parts: database migrations (rolling back code is easy, rolling back data/schema is not: use expand/contract, keep destructive changes a release later, take backups, forward-fix instead of reverse migrations); message schemas (new producers must stay readable by old consumers); externally visible side effects (emails sent); caches and sessions.
• Practice rollbacks regularly; define rollback criteria (SLO breach, error rate > X% for Y minutes); keep previous N versions available; write a deployment runbook and run post-deploy verification.
codeExamples:
# Helm
helm history catalogue -n prod
helm rollback catalogue 12 -n prod --wait

# Kubernetes
kubectl rollout undo deployment/catalogue --to-revision=7
kubectl rollout status deployment/catalogue

# GitOps (Argo CD): revert the commit that changed the image tag, Argo syncs the cluster back
git revert <deploy-commit> && git push

# Feature flag kill switch (no deployment)
curl -X PATCH https://flags.javaschoollab.com/api/flags/new-checkout -d '{"enabled": false}'

-- schema safety: expand first, contract later
-- release N:   ADD COLUMN new_status   (nullable)  <- old and new code both work
-- release N+1: backfill + switch reads/writes
-- release N+2: DROP COLUMN old_status  (only when rollback to N is no longer needed)

interviewQA: Blue-green vs canary?

Blue-green switches all traffic at once between two full environments (instant rollback, double capacity); canary shifts traffic gradually to the new version while monitoring metrics, limiting the impact of a bad release.
Why are database migrations the hardest part of rollbacks?
Code can be reverted instantly but data and schema changes cannot, and old and new versions overlap during rollouts; use expand/contract, backward-compatible changes and forward fixes.
What is the fastest way to roll back a problematic feature?
A feature flag kill switch: turning the flag off disables the behaviour immediately without redeploying; otherwise redeploy the previous version (rollout undo, Helm rollback, GitOps revert).

topics.name: Unit Testing, JUnit 5, Mockito, Spring Boot Test and Integration Testing

beginner.content:
Testing strategy for microservices

• Test at several levels (the test pyramid): many fast unit tests (pure logic, no Spring), slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest), integration tests with real infrastructure in containers, contract tests between services, a handful of end-to-end tests, plus performance and fault-injection tests. Avoid the "ice-cream cone" (mostly slow end-to-end tests).
• Principles: test behaviour not implementation; independent, repeatable, fast tests; arrange-act-assert; meaningful names; no shared mutable state; no sleeping (use Awaitility); real dependencies in containers rather than mocks where integration matters (databases, Kafka).
codeExamples:
Unit        : service/domain classes with Mockito       ms        thousands
Slice       : @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest (partial context)  100s of ms  hundreds
Integration : @SpringBootTest + Testcontainers (real DB/Kafka)  seconds  dozens
Contract    : provider verification + consumer stubs          seconds   per API
End-to-end  : deployed system, critical journeys only         minutes   a few

intermediate.content:
JUnit 5 and Mockito

• JUnit 5 (Jupiter): @Test, @BeforeEach, @ParameterizedTest (@CsvSource, @MethodSource), @Nested, @DisplayName, @Tag, assertions (assertThrows, assertAll) with AssertJ for fluent assertions. Mockito: @Mock, @InjectMocks, when(...).thenReturn, verify(mock).method(...), ArgumentCaptor, BDDMockito; use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) (strict stubs report unused stubbings).
• Mock collaborators (repositories, remote clients), not the class under test; do not over-mock (tests that mirror the implementation); prefer fakes for simple dependencies; do not mock value objects.

expert.content:
Spring Boot Test and slice tests

• @SpringBootTest starts the full application context (use webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT with TestRestTemplate/WebTestClient/RestTestClient); slow: use it for a few integration tests. Slice tests load only part: @WebMvcTest(Controller.class) (MVC + MockMvc, @MockitoBean services), @DataJpaTest (JPA + repositories, in a transaction rolled back), @JsonTest, @RestClientTest. @MockBean is replaced by @MockitoBean in Spring Boot 3.4+.
• Test security (spring-security-test: @WithMockUser, jwt()), validation and error responses (status + Problem Details), serialisation of DTOs, and repository queries against the real database type (not H2 if production is PostgreSQL).

interviewQA: Unit test vs slice test vs integration test in Spring Boot?

A unit test exercises one class without Spring; a slice test (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) loads only the relevant part of the context; an integration test (@SpringBootTest) starts the full application, ideally with real infrastructure in containers.
Why not test repositories against H2 when production uses PostgreSQL?
Dialect, SQL features, locking and constraint behaviour differ, so H2 can pass tests that fail in production; use Testcontainers with the real database engine.
What should you mock in a unit test?
Collaborators such as repositories and remote clients, not the class under test or simple value objects; avoid over-mocking that just mirrors the implementation.

topics.name: Testcontainers and WireMock

beginner.content:
Testcontainers

• Testcontainers starts real services (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Kafka, Redis, RabbitMQ, Keycloak, LocalStack, Elasticsearch) in Docker containers for tests: production-like, disposable, no shared test environment. With Spring Boot 3.1+ use @ServiceConnection (auto-wires the datasource/Kafka properties) or @DynamicPropertySource. Share containers across tests (singleton/static or reusable) to keep the suite fast; run Flyway migrations on the real DB.
• Docker must be available in CI (GitHub Actions ubuntu runners have it; Jenkins agents need a Docker socket or Testcontainers Cloud).

intermediate.content:
WireMock

• WireMock is an HTTP mock server: stub responses of other services (or third-party APIs: payment gateway) so your service can be tested in isolation: define request matchers (URL, headers, body) and canned responses, simulate failures (500, delays, connection reset, malformed body, fault injection), stateful scenarios (first call fails, second succeeds: test retries), and verify the calls made. Use @WireMockTest (JUnit 5) or spring-cloud-contract-wiremock/wiremock-spring-boot.
• Point the client base URL at the WireMock port via properties. Record/playback is useful for exploration but keep stubs hand-crafted for stability.

expert.content:
Combining them: a robust integration test setup

• Use Testcontainers for infrastructure you own (your database, broker, cache, auth server) and WireMock for other teams' services and third parties (you cannot start their whole stack). Together they let each service be tested in isolation but realistically in CI in a few minutes.
• Tips: one shared container setup (abstract base class or @ImportTestcontainers); reset state between tests (truncate tables, reset WireMock, purge topics); randomise ports; keep stubs near the tests; test timeouts, 5xx, slow, malformed responses explicitly; run in parallel carefully (isolated schemas/topics per test).

interviewQA: Why use Testcontainers instead of embedded databases?

Tests run against the same database engine and version as production (SQL dialect, locking, constraints, extensions), giving realistic results; containers are disposable and need no shared environment.
What is WireMock used for?

Stubbing HTTP dependencies (other services, third-party APIs) with controlled responses, delays and faults so a service can be tested in isolation, including retry and circuit-breaker behaviour, and verifying the requests it sends.
How do you test retry behaviour?
With WireMock scenarios: make the first call fail (500 or delay) and the next succeed, then assert the final result and verify the number of requests made.

topics.name: Contract Testing, Spring Cloud Contract, End-to-End, Performance and Fault-Injection Testing

beginner.content:
Contract testing

• Problem: service A calls service B; each team tests with mocks, but the mocks drift from reality, so integration breaks in staging. Consumer-driven contract testing: the consumer states what it needs (request → response); the provider verifies it still satisfies every consumer's contract in its own build. Breaking changes fail the provider's CI before deployment, without running both services together.
• Tools: Spring Cloud Contract (contracts in Groovy/YAML/Kotlin on the provider side; generates provider tests and WireMock stubs published as a jar for consumers), Pact (consumer-written pact files, a Pact Broker with can-i-deploy checks; polyglot), OpenAPI-based schema checks (Schemathesis, oasdiff for breaking-change detection).

intermediate.content:
End-to-end and performance testing

• End-to-end (E2E) tests drive the deployed system through the UI/API for a few critical journeys (sign up, enrol, pay, certificate): Playwright/Cypress/Selenium or REST-assured against staging with seeded data. They are slow and flaky, so keep few, make them independent and robust (wait for conditions), and use synthetic monitoring in production. Prefer consumer-driven contracts + integration tests for coverage.
• Performance testing: load (expected traffic), stress (beyond capacity to find breaking points), spike, soak/endurance (hours: memory leaks, connection leaks), and scalability tests. Tools: k6 (JavaScript), Gatling (Scala/Java DSL), JMeter, Locust. Define SLOs (p95 < 300 ms at 500 rps), test in a production-like environment with realistic data, watch metrics, traces and resource saturation during the run, make tests part of the pipeline (smoke-level on every release, full runs nightly).

expert.content:
Fault-injection and chaos testing

• Resilience patterns are only trustworthy if proven under failure. Fault-injection testing deliberately injects failures: latency, errors (500/503), dropped connections, timeouts, malformed responses, dependency outages, pod/node failures, network partitions, CPU/memory pressure, clock skew. Chaos engineering runs controlled experiments in staging (and carefully production): hypothesis ("if payments is down checkout still accepts orders") → inject → observe SLOs → fix.
• Tools: WireMock faults and Toxiproxy (network faults in integration tests with Testcontainers), Chaos Monkey for Spring Boot (assaults on latency/exceptions/kill app), Chaos Mesh / LitmusChaos / Gremlin (Kubernetes), Istio fault injection (HTTP delay/abort), AWS FIS. Verify: circuit breakers open, fallbacks work, retries do not storm, queues drain, alerts fire, runbooks work, recovery is automatic.

interviewQA: What is consumer-driven contract testing and why use it?

The consumer defines the requests and responses it relies on; the provider verifies these contracts in its own build. It catches breaking API changes before deployment without running all services together.
Spring Cloud Contract vs Pact?

Spring Cloud Contract is provider-driven (contracts in the provider repo, generates provider tests and WireMock stubs) and Spring-centric; Pact is consumer-driven, polyglot, with a Pact Broker and can-i-deploy checks. Both prevent consumer/provider drift.
Why do fault-injection and chaos tests matter?

They prove resilience mechanisms (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, fallbacks, autoscaling) actually work under failure, by injecting latency, errors and outages and checking that SLOs hold and recovery is automatic.

topics.name: Strangler Fig, Backend for Frontend and API Composition

beginner.content:
Strangler Fig pattern

• Incrementally replace a monolith: put a facade/proxy (gateway) in front; route one capability at a time to a new microservice while the rest still goes to the monolith; when a capability is fully migrated, delete it from the monolith; eventually the monolith is "strangled". Avoids risky big-bang rewrites.
• Steps: (1) identify a seam (a bounded context with few dependencies; e.g. notifications, catalogue search), (2) add the routing layer, (3) build the new service and synchronise data (CDC/events, dual-run, anti-corruption layer to translate models), (4) shadow/canary traffic and compare results, (5) switch, (6) remove old code and data. Migrate data ownership carefully (the hardest part: start with read-only data, then writes).
codeExamples:
Phase 1: all traffic -> monolith
Phase 2: gateway routes  /api/notifications/** -> new notification-service;  everything else -> monolith
Phase 3: more routes migrated (catalogue, assessment); monolith shrinks
Phase 4: monolith retired

# Spring Cloud Gateway: strangle by path, with a weighted canary for the new service
spring.cloud.gateway.routes:
  - id: notifications-new
    uri: lb://notification-service
    predicates: [ Path=/api/notifications/**, Weight=notif, 20 ]       # 20% to the new service
  - id: notifications-old
    uri: http://legacy-monolith:8080
    predicates: [ Path=/api/notifications/**, Weight=notif, 80 ]
  - id: legacy-default
    uri: http://legacy-monolith:8080
    predicates: [ Path=/** ]

intermediate.content:
Backend for Frontend (BFF)

• Different clients (web, mobile, partner API, smart TV) need different data shapes, payload sizes and auth flows. A BFF is a backend per frontend owned by that frontend's team: it aggregates calls to microservices, trims/reshapes responses, handles client-specific auth (the web BFF keeps tokens server-side and issues an HttpOnly session cookie), caches, and absorbs API changes. Avoids a one-size-fits-all gateway and overly chatty clients.
• Rules: keep the BFF thin (no core business logic), one per client type, owned by the client team, resilient (timeouts, fallbacks), and use the gateway for generic edge concerns (TLS, rate limiting) in front. Technologies: Spring Boot/WebFlux, Node.js/NestJS, GraphQL (a natural BFF), Spring Cloud Gateway MVC with aggregation.

expert.content:
API Composition

• Queries spanning several services (an order page needing order + customer + payment + shipment data) cannot use joins. API composition: a composer (gateway, BFF or an aggregator service) calls the owning services (in parallel), then joins the results in memory and returns one response. Simple and good for small/medium data and few services.
• Drawbacks: higher latency (slowest call dominates), reduced availability (needs timeouts/fallbacks and partial results), in-memory joins for large lists are inefficient, no cross-service consistency, N+1 call patterns (use batch endpoints: GET /customers?ids=...), no cross-service sorting/filtering. For heavy cross-service querying use CQRS read models/materialized views instead (next lesson).

interviewQA: What is the strangler fig pattern?
Gradually migrating a monolith by routing individual capabilities through a facade to new services and retiring the old code piece by piece, avoiding a risky big-bang rewrite.
What is a Backend for Frontend?
A thin backend dedicated to one client type (web, mobile) that aggregates and reshapes data from microservices and handles client-specific concerns, owned by that frontend's team.
When is API composition not enough?
When queries need joins, sorting or filtering across large datasets from several services, because in-memory composition is slow and fragile; use CQRS read models or materialized views.

topics.name: Event Sourcing, Anti-Corruption Layer and Materialized Views

beginner.content:
Event Sourcing

• Instead of storing the current state, store the sequence of events that led to it (OrderPlaced, ItemAdded, OrderPaid) in an append-only event store; current state = replay (fold) of events. Benefits: complete audit log, time travel/temporal queries, easy projections for new read models (replay history), natural fit with CQRS and event-driven integration, debugging by replay. Costs: learning curve, event schema evolution (upcasters), eventual consistency of projections, storage growth (use snapshots), complex queries need projections, GDPR deletion (crypto-shredding).
• Use for domains where history matters (finance, orders, compliance); do not use it everywhere. Tools: Axon Framework/Axon Server, EventStoreDB, Kafka as a log (with care), a PostgreSQL events table, Marten (.NET).

intermediate.content:
Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)

• When integrating with a legacy system, third-party API or another team's model you do not want its concepts, naming and quirks leaking into your domain. An anti-corruption layer is a translation boundary: adapters/facades + translators/mappers convert between the external model and your own domain model, so changes on the other side affect only the ACL. Essential in strangler migrations (new service ↔ monolith) and when wrapping payment gateways, ERP, SOAP services.
• Implementation: define a port (interface in your domain language: PaymentProvider.charge(Money, Card)), implement it with an adapter that calls the external API and maps request/response/errors/status codes into domain types; keep mapping code and external DTOs inside the adapter package; this is the Hexagonal idea applied to integration.

expert.content:
Materialized views

• A materialized view is a pre-computed, stored result of a query (denormalised) that is refreshed as source data changes, trading storage and staleness for fast reads. In microservices it is the standard way to answer cross-service queries without runtime joins: a service subscribes to events of several services and maintains its own read-optimised table/document/index (the read side of CQRS), e.g. order_summary with customer name, course titles and payment status in one row.
• Maintaining them: event-driven projections (idempotent handlers, versioned, rebuildable by replaying the event log), CDC (Debezium → Kafka → projector), database materialized views (REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY, scheduled or triggered), search indexes (Elasticsearch), caches (Redis). Handle rebuilds (reset + replay), lag monitoring, idempotency, out-of-order events (versions), and clear ownership (the projection owner is responsible for its correctness).

interviewQA: Event sourcing vs traditional state storage?

Event sourcing stores an append-only sequence of domain events and derives the current state by replaying them, giving a full audit trail and easy new projections but adding complexity (schema evolution, snapshots, eventual consistency). Traditional storage keeps only the latest state.
What is an anti-corruption layer?
A translation boundary (ports, adapters and mappers) that shields your domain model from the models, codes and quirks of legacy or third-party systems so changes there do not leak into your domain.
What is a materialized view used for in microservices?
To serve cross-service or heavy queries quickly from a pre-computed, denormalised read model that is kept up to date by events or CDC, avoiding runtime joins and distributed queries.

topics.name: Sidecar, Ambassador and Hexagonal Architecture

beginner.content:
Sidecar pattern

• A sidecar is a helper container deployed alongside the main application container in the same Pod (sharing network and volumes) providing cross-cutting capabilities without changing the app or its language: proxy/service mesh (Envoy in Istio/Linkerd: mTLS, retries, metrics), log shipping (Fluent Bit), config/secret refresh (Vault agent), certificate rotation, metrics exporters, Dapr (building blocks via a sidecar API: pub/sub, state, secrets), OAuth proxy. Benefits: polyglot support, separate lifecycle and ownership (platform team), consistent behaviour across services. Costs: extra resource use and latency, complexity, startup/shutdown ordering (Kubernetes native sidecar containers in 1.29+ solve ordering).
codeExamples:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: catalogue }
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: catalogue                                   # the application
          image: ghcr.io/javaschoollab/catalogue-service:1.4.2
          volumeMounts: [ { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log/app } ]
        - name: log-shipper                                 # sidecar: ships logs written by the app
          image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
          volumeMounts: [ { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log/app, readOnly: true } ]
      initContainers:
        - name: envoy-proxy                                 # Kubernetes native sidecar (1.29+): starts first, runs for the pod's lifetime
          image: envoyproxy/envoy:v1.31
          restartPolicy: Always
      volumes: [ { name: logs, emptyDir: {} } ]

# Istio injects an Envoy sidecar automatically: kubectl label namespace jsl istio-injection=enabled

intermediate.content:
Ambassador pattern

• An ambassador is a helper (often a sidecar) that acts as an out-of-process proxy for outgoing connections from the app to remote services: it handles retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, TLS/mTLS, authentication, routing/service discovery, rate limiting, request logging and tracing so the application just calls localhost:port. Typical uses: legacy apps that cannot be modified, polyglot fleets needing uniform resilience, connecting to databases/brokers through a secure proxy (Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, Envoy), offloading client-side concerns.
• Sidecar vs ambassador: sidecar = general "helper next to the app"; ambassador = a specific role of the helper: represents the app to the outside (egress proxy). A service mesh combines both (Envoy handles ingress and egress).
codeExamples:
# Cloud SQL / database access via an ambassador proxy in the pod
containers:
  - name: app
    image: ghcr.io/javaschoollab/reporting:2.0.1
    env: [ { name: DB_URL, value: "jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:5432/reporting" } ]       # the app talks to localhost
  - name: db-proxy                                           # ambassador: authenticated, encrypted tunnel to the real database
    image: gcr.io/cloud-sql-connectors/cloud-sql-proxy:2.11
    args: ["--private-ip", "jsl-project:asia-south1:reporting-db"]

# Envoy ambassador config idea: the app calls http://localhost:9001, Envoy adds retries/timeouts/mTLS to payment-service
# route: { timeout: 2s, retry_policy: { retry_on: "5xx,connect-failure", num_retries: 2, per_try_timeout: 0.8s } }

expert.content:
Hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters)

• Hexagonal architecture (Alistair Cockburn; also Clean/Onion) keeps the domain/application core independent of technology. The core defines ports (interfaces): inbound/driving ports (use cases: EnrollStudent) and outbound/driven ports (EnrollmentRepository, PaymentProvider, EventPublisher). Adapters implement them: inbound adapters (REST controller, Kafka listener, CLI) call use cases; outbound adapters (JPA, Kafka producer, HTTP client) implement the driven ports. Dependencies point inward: the domain knows nothing about Spring, JPA or HTTP.
• Benefits: testable core (unit-test use cases with fake adapters, no containers), replaceable infrastructure (swap Kafka for RabbitMQ, JPA for jOOQ), clear boundaries inside a microservice, easier to evolve and to move to/from a monolith. Costs: more interfaces and mapping; do not over-engineer simple CRUD services.
• Package layout: domain (entities, value objects, domain services), application (use cases + ports), adapter.in.web, adapter.out.persistence, adapter.out.messaging, config. Enforce with ArchUnit tests.

interviewQA: What is the sidecar pattern?

Deploying a helper container beside the application container in the same pod to provide cross-cutting capabilities (proxying/mTLS, log shipping, secret refresh) without changing the application code.
What is hexagonal architecture?

An architecture where the domain core is isolated behind ports (interfaces) and technology is attached through adapters (REST, JPA, messaging), with dependencies pointing inward so the core is testable and infrastructure replaceable.
Sidecar vs ambassador?

A sidecar is any helper container alongside the app; an ambassador is a specific kind of helper that acts as an outbound proxy on behalf of the app, adding retries, TLS, routing and resilience to its remote calls.

topics.name: Interview Q&A: Architecture, Communication and Resilience (159-165)

beginner.content:
How to answer microservices questions

• Interviewers look for trade-off thinking: state the pattern, when to use it and when not, a concrete Spring Boot/Kafka/Kubernetes implementation, and the failure modes. Use a real example (order, payment, enrolment) and mention monitoring and testing.
• Questions here: monolith vs microservices, how services communicate, how Eureka works, what an API gateway is, how a circuit breaker works, the Saga pattern, distributed transactions.

intermediate.content:
Model answers

QuestionAnswer
Monolith vs microservicesA monolith is one deployable with one database: simple to build, test and deploy at small scale. Microservices are independently deployable services around business capabilities, each owning its data: independent scaling and releases and team autonomy, at the cost of distributed-system complexity (network failures, data consistency, operations). Start with a modular monolith; split when boundaries and needs are clear.
How do microservices communicate?Synchronously via REST/gRPC (RestClient, WebClient, OpenFeign) for queries and immediate answers, with timeouts, retries and circuit breakers; asynchronously via events/messages (Kafka, RabbitMQ) for decoupling and eventual consistency, with idempotent consumers and the outbox pattern.
How does Eureka work?Services register with the Eureka server (name, host, port, health URL) and renew a lease with heartbeats; the server evicts expired leases and replicates to peers. Clients fetch and cache the registry and use a client-side load balancer to pick an instance. Self-preservation mode avoids mass eviction during network problems. On Kubernetes, Services/DNS replace it.
What is an API Gateway?The single entry point that routes requests to services and centralises cross-cutting concerns: authentication (JWT validation), rate limiting, TLS, CORS, logging/tracing and resilience filters. Spring Cloud Gateway uses routes (predicates + filters). Keep it thin and run several instances.
How does a circuit breaker work?It monitors calls; when the failure/slow-call rate exceeds a threshold it opens and fails fast (optionally returning a fallback) for a wait period, then half-opens to allow trial calls and closes again if they succeed. Resilience4j implements it (with retry, timeout, bulkhead, rate limiter).
What is the Saga pattern?A sequence of local transactions across services, each triggering the next via events or commands, with compensating transactions to undo previous steps on failure. Choreography (event-driven) or orchestration (central coordinator). Results in eventual consistency; compensations must be idempotent.
How do you handle distributed transactions?Avoid 2PC; use sagas with compensations, the transactional outbox for reliable event publishing, idempotent consumers, and design aggregates so one transaction affects one service; accept eventual consistency and expose pending states.

expert.content:
Likely follow-up questions

• "What happens if payment succeeds but publishing PaymentCompleted fails?" → the outbox: the event is stored in the same DB transaction and relayed later.
• "How do you stop a slow service from taking down the whole system?" → timeouts, bulkheads, circuit breakers, async events, load shedding, fallbacks.
• "When would you not use microservices?" → small team, unclear domain, low operational maturity: use a modular monolith.
• "How do you version APIs and events without breaking consumers?" → additive changes, tolerant readers, versioned endpoints/topics, schema registry, consumer-driven contracts.

interviewQA: Monolith vs microservices?

Monolith: one deployable, simple, ACID, scales as a whole; microservices: independently deployable, scalable and owned services with database per service, at the cost of distributed complexity. Choose based on team size, domain clarity and operational maturity.
How do you handle distributed transactions?
Use the saga pattern with compensating transactions (choreography or orchestration), the transactional outbox for reliable events and idempotent consumers; avoid 2PC and accept eventual consistency.
How does a circuit breaker help?
It fails fast when a dependency is unhealthy, protecting threads and latency, lets the dependency recover, and enables fallbacks; it moves through closed, open and half-open states.

topics.name: Interview Q&A: Security, Observability, Consistency and Operations (166-173)

beginner.content:
Questions 166-173

• How do you secure microservices? How do you trace requests across services? How do you prevent duplicate message processing? How do you handle service failures? How do you resolve database consistency issues? How do you prevent cascading failures? How do you deploy microservices independently? How do you troubleshoot production issues?
• Strong answers combine principles + tooling + a concrete incident.

intermediate.content:
Model answers

QuestionAnswer
How do you secure microservices?Centralised identity (OAuth2/OIDC, Keycloak); JWT validated at the gateway and in every service (zero trust); service-to-service auth with client credentials or mTLS; RBAC and method-level security plus ownership checks; TLS everywhere; secrets in Vault/secret managers; network policies; rate limiting; dependency/image scanning; audit logging.
How do you trace requests across services?Instrument with OpenTelemetry/Micrometer Tracing, propagate W3C traceparent through HTTP and message headers, export to Jaeger/Tempo/Zipkin, include trace ids in logs and error responses so logs, metrics and traces correlate; sample sensibly (tail sampling for errors/slow).
How do you prevent duplicate message processing?Idempotent consumers: inbox table with unique message id in the same transaction, naturally idempotent upserts/conditional updates, idempotency keys for APIs, producer idempotence, commit offsets after processing, DLQ for poison messages.
How do you handle service failures?Timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter for idempotent calls, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fallbacks/graceful degradation, asynchronous messaging, health probes with automatic restart/replacement, redundancy across zones, and runbooks/alerts.
How do you resolve database consistency issues?Keep one owner per piece of data; use sagas/outbox for cross-service flows; reconcile with periodic jobs and compensating actions; detect drift with consistency checks; optimistic locking inside a service; make operations idempotent; define acceptable consistency windows.
How do you prevent cascading failures?Timeouts shorter than callers', circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiting/load shedding, retry budgets with jitter, async decoupling, caches/fallbacks, autoscaling and capacity limits; verify with chaos tests.
How do you deploy microservices independently?Per-service repo/pipeline and versioned image; backward-compatible APIs, events and DB schema (expand/contract); contract tests; rolling/canary/blue-green with health gates; feature flags; GitOps; automated rollback.
How do you troubleshoot production issues?Start from alerts/SLO dashboards (RED metrics), find the failing service and time window, follow traces to the slow/failing hop, read correlated logs by trace id, check recent deployments/config changes, dependencies (DB pool, Kafka lag, breakers), resource saturation and thread/heap dumps; mitigate first (rollback, scale, flag off), then root-cause and write a post-mortem.

expert.content:
A production troubleshooting walkthrough

• Symptom: users report slow enrolment; alert "p95 latency > 1 s for 10 min" on learning-service.
• 1. Scope: Grafana RED dashboard: error rate normal, latency up only for POST /enrollments, started 14:05. 2. Recent change: deployment of catalogue-service v1.5.0 at 14:03. 3. Trace: slow traces show 900 ms in catalogue-service GET /courses/{id} → a new query without an index. 4. Dependencies: Hikari pool of catalogue at 100% active, circuit breaker in learning still closed but slow-call rate climbing. 5. Mitigate: roll back catalogue (rollout undo) or raise the flag off. 6. Fix: add the index via migration, add a query-count/perf test, adjust the breaker's slow-call threshold and timeouts, write the post-mortem.

# useful commands during an incident
kubectl get pods -n jsl -o wide && kubectl top pods -n jsl
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n jsl                       # events: OOMKilled? probe failures? image pull?
kubectl logs <pod> -n jsl --previous                    # logs of the crashed container
kubectl rollout history deploy/catalogue -n jsl && kubectl rollout undo deploy/catalogue -n jsl
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- jcmd 1 Thread.print           # thread dump (blocked threads, pool exhaustion)
curl -s localhost:9090/actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.pending
# PromQL: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m])))
# Kibana: trace.id:"<id>" and log.level:ERROR

interviewQA: How do you troubleshoot production issues in microservices?

Begin with alerts and RED dashboards to scope the problem, correlate with recent deployments, follow distributed traces to the slow or failing hop, read logs by trace id, check dependencies and resource saturation (DB pool, Kafka lag, breakers, memory/threads), mitigate first (rollback, scale, flag off) and then root-cause and document.
How do you prevent cascading failures?
Timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiting and load shedding, retries with backoff and budgets, asynchronous decoupling, fallbacks and capacity limits, verified by fault-injection tests.
How do you secure a microservices system end to end?

Centralised OAuth2/OIDC identity, JWT validation in gateway and services, service-to-service authentication (client credentials/mTLS), RBAC and ownership checks, TLS, managed secrets, network policies, scanning in CI and audit logging.

topics.name: Example: Resilient Service Call with Timeout, Retry, Circuit Breaker and Fallback

beginner.content:
What you build

• An order-service calling an inventory-service over HTTP with a timeout, retry with backoff, a circuit breaker and a fallback, using Spring Boot 3 and Resilience4j.

intermediate.content:
Rules that make it safe

• Retry only idempotent calls (GET, or POST with an idempotency key). • Timeouts must be shorter than the caller's own timeout, and retries multiply load: use backoff + jitter. • The fallback must be a real business decision (cached value, default, queue for later), not an empty value that hides failures. • Expose breaker state through Actuator (/actuator/circuitbreakers).
codeExamples:
# watch the breaker
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,circuitbreakers,metrics
management.health.circuitbreakers.enabled: true
# metrics: resilience4j_circuitbreaker_state, resilience4j_circuitbreaker_failure_rate

expert.content: Testing the failure path

interviewQA: What are the dangers of naive retries?
Retrying non-idempotent calls duplicates side effects and synchronised retries amplify load; use idempotency keys, exponential backoff with jitter and limits.
What makes a good fallback?
A deliberate degraded behaviour such as a cached value or deferred processing, not a silent default that hides the outage.

topics.name: Example: Order Placement with Transactional Outbox and Idempotent Consumer

beginner.content:
What you build

• Order-service saves an order and an outbox row in one local transaction; a relay publishes the event to Kafka; payment-service consumes it idempotently. This is the building block of sagas without distributed transactions.

intermediate.content:
Idempotent consumer

• Delivery is at least once, so the consumer must handle duplicates: record processed event ids in a table with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the business change.

expert.content:
Compensation and failure handling

• If payment fails, payment-service emits PaymentFailed and order-service compensates (cancels the order): that is a choreographed saga. Add a dead-letter topic for poison messages, retry with backoff before the DLT, and monitor consumer lag and outbox backlog. Alternatives to a polling relay: CDC with Debezium reading the outbox table.

interviewQA: Why is the transactional outbox needed?
Writing to the database and publishing to a broker are two operations that cannot be atomic; the outbox stores the event in the same local transaction and a relay publishes it reliably.
How do you handle duplicate messages?
Make consumers idempotent by recording processed event ids with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the business update.

topics.name: Real-World Scenario: E-Commerce Checkout Across Services (Design Decisions)

beginner.content:
The scenario

• Checkout touches Order, Inventory, Payment, Notification and Shipping services, each with its own database. A customer clicks "Pay": what must be synchronous (the user waits) and what can be asynchronous (events)? A common answer: the API gateway calls Order synchronously (validate, create PENDING order, return 202 with an order id); the rest of the flow runs as an orchestrated or choreographed saga and the client polls or receives a push for the final status.
codeExamples:
Client -> Gateway -> Order Service:  POST /orders (Idempotency-Key)  => 202 Accepted { orderId, status: PENDING }

Order Service      --OrderPlaced-->         Inventory Service  (reserve stock)
Inventory Service  --StockReserved-->       Payment Service    (charge)
Payment Service    --PaymentCaptured-->     Order Service      (mark CONFIRMED) --> Shipping, Notification
   failure paths (compensation):
Payment Service    --PaymentFailed-->       Inventory Service  (release stock) --> Order Service (mark CANCELLED)
Inventory Service  --StockUnavailable-->    Order Service      (mark CANCELLED, tell customer)

intermediate.content:
Key decisions and why

DecisionChoiceReason
ConsistencySaga with compensationsNo distributed transactions across databases
Event reliabilityTransactional outbox + idempotent consumersAt-least-once delivery without lost or duplicate effects
Double click on PayIdempotency-Key headerSame request returns the same order
Payment gateway timeoutQuery payment status before retryingAvoid double charge
Read model for "My orders"CQRS view fed by eventsFast queries without joining services
Slow downstreamTimeouts, circuit breaker, bulkheadsProtect checkout from a failing service
Tracing a failed orderCorrelation id in every message and logOne id to follow the saga across services

expert.content:
Operating it

• Observability: distributed traces (OpenTelemetry), metrics (orders/minute, saga duration, DLQ size, outbox lag), structured logs with the order id. • Failure drills: kill payment-service mid-saga and verify compensation; replay a message twice and verify idempotency. • Operations: a dead-letter queue dashboard and a "stuck saga" job that times out PENDING orders after N minutes.

interviewQA: Why return 202 Accepted from checkout?
The multi-service saga completes asynchronously, so the API acknowledges the request and the client polls or is notified of the final status.
How do you handle a payment timeout?
Do not blindly retry: query the payment provider for the transaction status (or use an idempotency key) so the customer is never charged twice.
